{{see also|Oceanic carbon cycle}}In 2021, atmospheric carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) levels of around 415&nbsp;ppm were around 50% higher than preindustrial concentrations.<ref name="carbon budget 2022">{{cite journal |last1=Friedlingstein |first1=Pierre |last2=O'Sullivan |first2=Michael |last3=Jones |first3=Matthew W. |last4=Andrew |first4=Robbie M. |last5=Gregor |first5=Luke |last6=Hauck |first6=Judith |last7=Le Quéré |first7=Corinne |last8=Luijkx |first8=Ingrid T. |last9=Olsen |first9=Are |last10=Peters |first10=Glen P. |last11=Peters |first11=Wouter |last12=Pongratz |first12=Julia |last13=Schwingshackl |first13=Clemens |last14=Sitch |first14=Stephen |last15=Canadell |first15=Josep G. |date=2022-11-11 |title=Global Carbon Budget 2022 |journal=Earth System Science Data |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=4811–4900 |bibcode=2022ESSD...14.4811F |doi=10.5194/essd-14-4811-2022 |doi-access=free}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=16 October 2017}}</ref> According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in 2023, atmospheric {{CO2}} levels have risen from approximately 280 parts per million (ppm) in the pre-industrial era to over 410&nbsp;ppm today, primarily due to human activities such as fossil fuel combustion and deforestation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Çelekli |first1=Abuzer |last2=Zariç |first2=Özgür Eren |date=2024-12-31 |title=Rising tide of ocean acidification |url=http://dergipark.org.tr/en/doi/10.35208/ert.1407588 |journal=Environmental Research and Technology |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=605–613 |doi=10.35208/ert.1407588 |issn=2636-8498}}</ref> The current elevated levels and rapid growth rates are unprecedented in the past 55&nbsp;million years of the geological record. The sources of this excess {{CO2}} are clearly established as human driven: they include anthropogenic fossil fuel, industrial, and land-use/land-change emissions. One source of this is fossil fuels, which are burned for energy. When burned, {{CO2}} is released into the atmosphere as a byproduct of combustion, which is a significant contributor to the increasing levels of {{CO2}} in the Earth's atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Doney |first1=Scott C. |last2=Fabry |first2=Victoria J. |last3=Feely |first3=Richard A. |last4=Kleypas |first4=Joan A. |date=2009-01-01 |title=Ocean Acidification: The Other CO 2 Problem |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163834 |journal=Annual Review of Marine Science |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=169–192 |doi=10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163834 |issn=1941-1405 |pmid=21141034 |archive-date=29 December 2021 |access-date=11 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229064622/https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163834 |url-status=live}}</ref> The ocean acts as a [[carbon sink]] for anthropogenic {{CO2}} and takes up roughly a quarter of total anthropogenic {{CO2}} emissions.<ref name=":14">{{cite journal |last1=Doney |first1=Scott C. |last2=Busch |first2=D. Shallin |last3=Cooley |first3=Sarah R. |last4=Kroeker |first4=Kristy J. |date=2020-10-17 |title=The Impacts of Ocean Acidification on Marine Ecosystems and Reliant Human Communities |journal=Annual Review of Environment and Resources |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=83–112 |doi=10.1146/annurev-environ-012320-083019 |s2cid=225741986 |doi-access=free}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50x50px]] Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [[creativecommons:by/4.0/|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]</ref> However, the additional {{CO2}} in the ocean results in a wholesale shift in [[seawater]] acid-base chemistry toward more acidic, lower pH conditions and lower saturation states for carbonate minerals used in many marine organism shells and skeletons.<ref name=":14"/>

Accumulated since 1850, the ocean sink holds up to {{val|175|35|ul=gigatons}} of carbon, with more than two-thirds of this amount ({{val|120|ul=Gt}} C) being taken up by the global ocean since 1960. Over the historical period, the ocean sink increased in pace with the exponential anthropogenic emissions increase. From 1850 until 2022, the ocean has absorbed 26% of total anthropogenic emissions.<ref name="carbon budget 2022"/> Emissions during the period 1850–2021 amounted to {{val|670|65|u=gigatons}} of carbon and were partitioned among the atmosphere (41%), ocean (26%), and land (31%).<ref name="carbon budget 2022"/>

The [[carbon cycle]] describes the fluxes of carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) between the oceans, [[Earth|terrestrial]] [[biosphere]], [[lithosphere]],<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=carbon cycle |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica |url=http://www.search.eb.com/eb/article-9020247 |access-date=11 February 2010}}</ref> and [[atmosphere]]. The carbon cycle involves both [[organic compound]]s such as [[cellulose]] and inorganic carbon compounds such as [[carbon dioxide]], [[carbonate|carbonate ion]], and [[bicarbonate|bicarbonate ion]], together referenced as dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC). These inorganic compounds are particularly significant in ocean acidification, as they include many forms of dissolved {{CO2}} present in the Earth's oceans.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kump |first1=Lee R. |title=The Earth System |last2=Kasting |first2=James F. |author-link2=James Kasting |last3=Crane |first3=Robert G. |year=2003 |edition=2nd |pages=162–164 |publisher=Prentice Hall |location=Upper Saddle River, NJ |isbn=978-0-613-91814-5}}</ref>

When {{CO2}} dissolves, it reacts with water to form a balance of ionic and non-ionic chemical species: dissolved free carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}(aq)), [[carbonic acid]] ({{chem2|H2CO3}}), [[bicarbonate]] ({{chem2|HCO3-}}) and carbonate ({{chem2|CO3(2−)}}). The ratio of these species depends on factors such as [[seawater]] [[temperature]], pressure, and salinity (as shown in a [[Bjerrum plot]]). These different forms of [[total inorganic carbon|dissolved inorganic carbon]] are transferred from the ocean's surface to its interior by the ocean's [[solubility pump]]. The resistance of an area of ocean to absorbing atmospheric {{CO2}} is known as the [[Revelle factor]].

==Main effects==
The [[marine chemistry|ocean's chemistry]] is changing due to the uptake of anthropogenic carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}).<ref name="Jian2019">{{cite journal |last1=Jiang |first1=Li-Qing |last2=Carter |first2=Brendan R. |last3=Feely |first3=Richard A. |last4=Lauvset |first4=Siv K. |last5=Olsen |first5=Are |date=2019 |title=Surface ocean pH and buffer capacity: past, present and future |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=18624 |bibcode=2019NatSR...918624J |doi=10.1038/s41598-019-55039-4 |pmc=6901524 |pmid=31819102 |doi-access=free}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=16 October 2017}}</ref><ref name=":43">Cooley, S., D. Schoeman, L. Bopp, P. Boyd, S. Donner, D.Y. Ghebrehiwet, S.-I. Ito, W. Kiessling, P. Martinetto, E. Ojea, M.-F. Racault, B. Rost, and M. Skern-Mauritzen, 2022: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Chapter03.pdf Chapter 3: Oceans and Coastal Ecosystems and Their Services] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021104519/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGII_Chapter03.pdf |date=21 October 2022}}. In: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/ Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability. Contribution of Working Group II to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220228114918/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/ |date=28 February 2022}} [H.-O. Pörtner, D.C. Roberts, M. Tignor, E.S. Poloczanska, K. Mintenbeck, A. Alegría, M. Craig, S. Langsdorf, S. Löschke, V. Möller, A. Okem, B. Rama (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK and New York, NY, US, pp. 379–550.</ref>{{rp|395}} Ocean pH, carbonate ion concentrations ({{chem2|[CO3(2−)]}}), and calcium carbonate mineral saturation states (Ω) have been declining as a result of the uptake of approximately 30% of the anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions over the past 270 years (since around 1750). This process, commonly referred to as "ocean acidification", is making it harder for [[marine biogenic calcification|marine calcifiers]] to build a shell or skeletal structure, endangering coral reefs and the broader marine ecosystems.<ref name="Jian2019"/>

Ocean acidification has been called the "evil twin of [[global warming]]" and "the other {{CO2}} problem".<ref name="rsc">{{cite web |last=Notman |first=Nina |date=29 July 2014 |title=The other carbon dioxide problem |url=http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/2014/07/ocean-acidification |website=Chemistry World |access-date=22 December 2014 |archive-date=5 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160605110016/http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/2014/07/ocean-acidification |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Rogers |first=Alex |date=9 October 2013 |title=Global warming's evil twin: ocean acidification |url=http://theconversation.com/global-warmings-evil-twin-ocean-acidification-19017 |website=The Conversation |access-date=22 December 2014 |archive-date=1 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231001190748/https://theconversation.com/global-warmings-evil-twin-ocean-acidification-19017 |url-status=live}}</ref> Increased ocean temperatures and oxygen loss act concurrently with ocean acidification and constitute the "deadly trio" of climate change pressures on the marine environment.<ref>{{cite web |date=November 2017 |title=Ocean acidification (Issues Brief) |url=https://www.iucn.org/sites/dev/files/ocean_acidification_issues_brief.pdf |access-date=3 November 2020 |website=IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature) |archive-date=30 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201230063843/https://www.iucn.org/sites/dev/files/ocean_acidification_issues_brief.pdf}}</ref> The impacts of this will be most severe for coral reefs and other shelled marine organisms,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brander |first1=Luke M. |last2=Rehdanz |first2=Katrin |last3=Tol |first3=Richard S. J. |last4=Van Beukering |first4=Pieter J. H. |date=2012-02-01 |title=The economic impact of ocean acidification on coral reefs |journal=Climate Change Economics |volume=03 |issue=1 |page=1250002 |doi=10.1142/S2010007812500029 |bibcode=2012ClChE...350002B |hdl-access=free |hdl=2262/27779 |url=https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/4f6326ec-b0ff-4431-a201-cac1e7a0b7dd}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Allemand |first1=Denis |last2=Osborn |first2=David |date=2019 |title=Ocean acidification impacts on coral reefs: From sciences to solutions |journal=Regional Studies in Marine Science |volume=28 |article-number=100558 |bibcode=2019RSMS...2800558A |doi=10.1016/j.rsma.2019.100558 |s2cid=135282569 |doi-access=free}}</ref> as well as those populations that depend on the ecosystem services they provide.

===Reduction in pH value===
{{See also|Ocean#pH}}
Dissolving {{CO2}} in seawater increases the [[hydrogen]] ion ({{chem2|H+}}) concentration in the ocean, and thus decreases ocean pH, as follows:<ref name="IPCC">{{cite book |last1=Freund |first1=Paul |url=http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/special-reports/srccs/srccs_wholereport.pdf |title=IPCC Special Report on Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage |last2=Bachu |first2=Stefan |last3=Simbeck |first3=Dale |last4=Thambimuthu |first4=Kelly (Kailai) |last5=Gupta |first5=Murlidhar |publisher=IPCC |year=2005 |editor-last=Metz |editor-first=Bert |page=390 |chapter=Annex I: Properties of {{CO2}} and carbon-based fuels |access-date=1 November 2014 |editor-last2=Davidson |editor-first2=Ogunlade |editor-last3=de Coninck |editor-first3=Heleen |editor-last4=Loos |editor-first4=Manuela |editor-last5=Meyer |editor-first5=Leo |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100210022620/http://www.ipcc.ch/pdf/special-reports/srccs/srccs_wholereport.pdf |archive-date=10 February 2010}}</ref>
:{{chem2|CO2 <sub>(aq)</sub> + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ HCO3− + H+ ⇌ CO3(2−) + 2 H+.}}

In shallow coastal and shelf regions, a number of factors interplay to affect air-ocean {{CO2}} exchange and resulting pH change.<ref name="Carstensen2019">{{cite journal |last1=Carstensen |first1=Jacob |last2=Duarte |first2=Carlos M. |date=2019-04-16 |title=Drivers of pH Variability in Coastal Ecosystems |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |volume=53 |issue=8 |pages=4020–4029 |bibcode=2019EnST...53.4020C |doi=10.1021/acs.est.8b03655 |pmid=30892892 |s2cid=84841808}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Duarte |first1=Carlos M. |last2=Hendriks |first2=Iris E. |last3=Moore |first3=Tommy S. |last4=Olsen |first4=Ylva S. |last5=Steckbauer |first5=Alexandra |last6=Ramajo |first6=Laura |last7=Carstensen |first7=Jacob |last8=Trotter |first8=Julie A. |last9=McCulloch |first9=Malcolm |date=2013-03-01 |title=Is Ocean Acidification an Open-Ocean Syndrome? Understanding Anthropogenic Impacts on Seawater pH |journal=Estuaries and Coasts |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=221–236 |doi=10.1007/s12237-013-9594-3 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2013EstCo..36..221D}}</ref> These include biological processes, such as [[photosynthesis]] and respiration,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lowe |first1=Alexander T. |last2=Bos |first2=Julia |last3=Ruesink |first3=Jennifer |date=2019-01-30 |title=Ecosystem metabolism drives pH variability and modulates long-term ocean acidification in the Northeast Pacific coastal ocean |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=963 |bibcode=2019NatSR...9..963L |doi=10.1038/s41598-018-37764-4  |doi-access=free|pmc=6353961 |pmid=30700764}}</ref> as well as water upwelling.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fairchild |first1=William |last2=Hales |first2=Burke |date=2021 |title=High-Resolution Carbonate System Dynamics of Netarts Bay, OR From 2014 to 2019 |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=7 |article-number=590236 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2020.590236 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrMaS...790236F}}</ref> Also, [[stream metabolism|ecosystem metabolism]] in freshwater sources reaching coastal waters can lead to large, but local, pH changes.<ref name="Carstensen2019"/>

Freshwater bodies also appear to be acidifying, although this is a more complex and less obvious phenomenon.<ref name="Gies2018">{{cite web |last=Gies |first=E. |date=11 January 2018 |title=Like Oceans, Freshwater Is Also Acidifying |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/like-oceans-freshwater-is-also-acidifying/ |access-date=2018-01-13 |website=[[Scientific American]] |archive-date=15 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240115032023/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/like-oceans-freshwater-is-also-acidifying/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Weiss2018">{{cite journal |last1=Weiss |first1=L. C. |last2=Pötter |first2=L. |last3=Steiger |first3=A. |last4=Kruppert |first4=S. |last5=Frost |first5=U. |last6=Tollrian |first6=R. |year=2018 |title=Rising p{{CO2}} in Freshwater Ecosystems Has the Potential to Negatively Affect Predator-Induced Defenses in ''Daphnia'' |journal=Current Biology |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=327–332.e3 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2017.12.022 |pmid=29337079 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018CBio...28E.327W}}</ref>

The absorption of {{CO2}} from the atmosphere does not affect the ocean's [[alkalinity]].<ref name="IPCC AR6 WGI Glossary"/>{{rp|2252}} This is important to know in this context as alkalinity is the capacity of [[water]] to resist [[freshwater acidification|acidification]].<ref>{{cite news |date=2014 |title=What is alkalinity? |url=https://www.water-research.net/index.php/the-role-of-alkalinity-citizen-monitoring |access-date=5 February 2018 |publisher=Water Research Center |archive-date=6 February 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180206002603/https://www.water-research.net/index.php/the-role-of-alkalinity-citizen-monitoring |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Ocean alkalinity enhancement]] has been proposed as one option to add alkalinity to the ocean and therefore buffer against pH changes.

===Decreased calcification in marine organisms===
[[File:Foraminifera (265 36) Various.jpg|thumb|Various types of [[foraminifera]] observed through a microscope using differential interference contrast]]
[[File:Carbonate system of seawater.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Bjerrum plot]]: Change in carbonate system of seawater from ocean acidification]]
Changes in ocean chemistry can have extensive direct and indirect effects on organisms and their habitats. One of the most important repercussions of increasing ocean acidity relates to the production of shells out of [[calcium carbonate]] ({{chem2|CaCO3}}).<ref name="raven05">{{cite book |url=https://royalsociety.org/-/media/Royal_Society_Content/policy/publications/2005/9634.pdf |title=Ocean acidification due to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide |publisher=Royal Society |year=2005 |isbn=0-85403-617-2 |archive-date=3 July 2023 |access-date=25 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230703013808/https://royalsociety.org/-/media/royal_society_content/policy/publications/2005/9634.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> This process is called calcification and is important to the biology and survival of a wide range of marine organisms. Calcification involves the [[precipitation (chemistry)|precipitation]] of dissolved ions into solid {{chem2|CaCO3}} structures, structures for many marine organisms, such as [[coccolithophore]]s, [[foraminifera]], [[crustacea]]ns, [[Mollusca|mollusks]], etc. After they are formed, these {{chem2|CaCO3}} structures are vulnerable to [[dissolution (chemistry)|dissolution]] unless the surrounding seawater contains [[saturated solution|saturating]] concentrations of carbonate ions ({{chem2|CO3(2−)}}).

Very little of the extra carbon dioxide that is added into the ocean remains as dissolved carbon dioxide. The majority dissociates into additional bicarbonate and free hydrogen ions. The increase in hydrogen is larger than the increase in bicarbonate,<ref name="Mitchell">{{cite journal |last1=Mitchell |first1=Mark J. |last2=Jensen |first2=Oliver E. |last3=Cliffe |first3=K. Andrew |last4=Maroto-Valer |first4=M. Mercedes |date=8 May 2010 |title=A model of carbon dioxide dissolution and mineral carbonation kinetics |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |volume=466 |issue=2117 |pages=1265–1290 |bibcode=2010RSPSA.466.1265M |doi=10.1098/rspa.2009.0349 |doi-access=free}}</ref> creating an imbalance in the reaction:
:{{chem2|HCO3− ⇌ CO3(2−) + H+}}
To maintain chemical equilibrium, some of the carbonate ions already in the ocean combine with some of the hydrogen ions to make further bicarbonate. Thus the ocean's concentration of carbonate ions is reduced, removing an essential building block for marine organisms to build shells, or calcify:
:{{chem2|Ca(2+) + CO3(2−) ⇌ CaCO3}}

The increase in concentrations of dissolved carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, and reduction in carbonate, are shown in the [[Bjerrum plot]].

Disruption of the food chain is also a possible effect as many marine organisms rely on calcium carbonate-based organisms at the base of the food chain for food and habitat. This can potentially have detrimental effects throughout the food web and potentially lead to a decline in availability of fish stocks which would have an impact on human livelihoods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kroeker |first1=Kristy J. |last2=Kordas |first2=Rebecca L. |last3=Crim |first3=Ryan |last4=Hendriks |first4=Iris E. |last5=Ramajo |first5=Laura |last6=Singh |first6=Gerald S. |last7=Duarte |first7=Carlos M. |last8=Gattuso |first8=Jean-Pierre |date=June 2013 |title=Impacts of ocean acidification on marine organisms: quantifying sensitivities and interaction with warming |journal=Global Change Biology |language=en |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=1884–1896 |bibcode=2013GCBio..19.1884K |doi=10.1111/gcb.12179 |issn=1354-1013 |pmc=3664023 |pmid=23505245}}</ref>

===Decrease in saturation state===
[[File:CalciumAragoniteSaturation.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|Distribution of (A) aragonite and (B) calcite saturation depth in the global oceans<ref name="Feely04">{{cite journal |last1=Feely |first1=Richard A. |last2=Sabine |first2=Christopher L. |last3=Lee |first3=Kitack |last4=Berelson |first4=Will |last5=Kleypas |first5=Joanie |last6=Fabry |first6=Victoria J. |last7=Millero |first7=Frank J. |date=16 July 2004 |title=Impact of Anthropogenic {{CO2}} on the CaCO<sub>3</sub> System in the Oceans |journal=Science |volume=305 |issue=5682 |pages=362–366 |bibcode=2004Sci...305..362F |doi=10.1126/science.1097329 |pmid=15256664 |s2cid=31054160}}</ref>]]
The [[saturated solution|saturation]] state (known as Ω) of seawater for a mineral is a measure of the thermodynamic potential for the mineral to form or to dissolve, and for calcium carbonate is described by the following equation:
:<math chem="">{\Omega} = \frac{\left[\ce{Ca^2+}\right] \left[\ce{CO3^2-}\right]}{K_{sp}}</math>

Here Ω is the product of the concentrations (or [[activity (chemistry)|activities]]) of the reacting ions that form the mineral ({{chem2|Ca2+ and CO3(2−)}}), divided by the apparent solubility product at [[chemical equilibrium|equilibrium]] (K<sub>sp</sub>), that is, when the rates of precipitation and dissolution are equal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Atkinson |first1=M.J. |last2=Cuet |first2=P. |year=2008 |title=Possible effects of ocean acidification on coral reef biogeochemistry: topics for research |journal=[[Marine Ecology Progress Series]] |volume=373 |pages=249–256 |bibcode=2008MEPS..373..249A |doi=10.3354/meps07867 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In seawater, dissolution boundary is formed as a result of temperature, pressure, and depth, and is known as the saturation horizon.<ref name="raven05"/> Above this saturation horizon,  has a value greater than 1, and {{chem2|CaCO3}} does not readily dissolve. Most calcifying organisms live in such waters.<ref name="raven05"/> Below this depth,  has a value less than 1, and {{chem2|CaCO3}} will dissolve. The [[carbonate compensation depth]] is the ocean depth at which carbonate dissolution balances the supply of carbonate to sea floor, therefore sediment below this depth will be void of calcium carbonate.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thurman |first1=H.V. |title=Introductory Oceanography |last2=Trujillo |first2=A.P. |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-13-143888-0}}</ref> Increasing {{CO2}} levels, and the resulting lower pH of seawater, decreases the concentration of {{chem2|CO3(2−)}} and the saturation state of {{chem2|CaCO3}} therefore increasing {{chem2|CaCO3}} dissolution.

Calcium carbonate most commonly occurs in two common [[polymorphism (materials science)|polymorphs]] (crystalline forms): [[aragonite]] and [[calcite]]. Aragonite is much more soluble than calcite, so the aragonite saturation horizon, and aragonite compensation depth, is always nearer to the surface than the calcite saturation horizon.<ref name="raven05"/> This also means that those organisms that produce aragonite may be more vulnerable to changes in ocean acidity than those that produce calcite.<ref name="orr05">{{cite journal |last1=Orr |first1=James C. |last2=Fabry |first2=Victoria J. |last3=Aumont |first3=Olivier |last4=Bopp |first4=Laurent |last5=Doney |first5=Scott C. |last6=Feely |first6=Richard A. |last7=Gnanadesikan |first7=Anand |last8=Gruber |first8=Nicolas |last9=Ishida |first9=Akio |last10=Joos |first10=Fortunat |last11=Key |first11=Robert M. |last12=Lindsay |first12=Keith |last13=Maier-Reimer |first13=Ernst |last14=Matear |first14=Richard |last15=Monfray |first15=Patrick |date=September 2005 |title=Anthropogenic ocean acidification over the twenty-first century and its impact on calcifying organisms |url=https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/13479/1/Orr2005a.pdf |journal=Nature |volume=437 |issue=7059 |pages=681–686 |bibcode=2005Natur.437..681O |doi=10.1038/nature04095 |pmid=16193043 |s2cid=4306199 |last16=Mouchet |first16=Anne |last17=Najjar |first17=Raymond G. |last18=Plattner |first18=Gian-Kasper |last19=Rodgers |first19=Keith B. |last20=Sabine |first20=Christopher L. |last21=Sarmiento |first21=Jorge L. |last22=Schlitzer |first22=Reiner |last23=Slater |first23=Richard D. |last24=Totterdell |first24=Ian J. |last25=Weirig |first25=Marie-France |last26=Yamanaka |first26=Yasuhiro |last27=Yool |first27=Andrew |archive-date=19 September 2020 |access-date=21 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919091116/https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/13479/1/Orr2005a.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> Ocean acidification and the resulting decrease in carbonate saturation states raise the saturation horizons of both forms closer to the surface.<ref name="raven05"/> This decrease in saturation state is one of the main factors leading to decreased calcification in marine organisms because the inorganic precipitation of {{chem2|CaCO3}} is directly proportional to its saturation state and calcifying organisms exhibit stress in waters with lower saturation states.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hofmann |first1=Gretchen E. |last2=Barry |first2=James P. |last3=Edmunds |first3=Peter J. |last4=Gates |first4=Ruth D. |last5=Hutchins |first5=David A. |last6=Klinger |first6=Terrie |last7=Sewell |first7=Mary A. |author7-link=Mary A. Sewell |date=2010-12-01 |title=The Effect of Ocean Acidification on Calcifying Organisms in Marine Ecosystems: An Organism-to-Ecosystem Perspective |journal=Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=127–147 |doi=10.1146/annurev.ecolsys.110308.120227}}</ref>

===Natural variability and climate feedbacks===
{{Further|Carbonate compensation depth}}

Already now large quantities of water undersaturated in [[aragonite]] are [[upwelling]] close to the Pacific [[continental shelf]] area of North America, from [[Vancouver]] to [[Northern California]].<ref name="feeley08">{{cite journal |last1=Feely |first1=Richard A. |last2=Sabine |first2=Christopher L. |last3=Hernandez-Ayon |first3=J. Martin |last4=Ianson |first4=Debby |last5=Hales |first5=Burke |date=13 June 2008 |title=Evidence for Upwelling of Corrosive "Acidified" Water onto the Continental Shelf |journal=Science |volume=320 |issue=5882 |pages=1490–1492 |bibcode=2008Sci...320.1490F |doi=10.1126/science.1155676 |pmid=18497259 |s2cid=35487689}}</ref> These continental shelves play an important role in marine ecosystems, since most [[marine organisms]] live or are [[spawn (biology)|spawned]] there. Other shelf areas may be experiencing similar effects.<ref name="feeley08"/>

At depths of 1000s of meters in the ocean, calcium carbonate shells begin to dissolve as increasing pressure and decreasing temperature shift the chemical equilibria controlling calcium carbonate precipitation.<ref name=":13">{{cite journal |last1=Boudreau |first1=Bernard P. |last2=Middelburg |first2=Jack J. |last3=Hofmann |first3=Andreas F. |last4=Meysman |first4=Filip J. R. |date=2010 |title=Ongoing transients in carbonate compensation |journal=Global Biogeochemical Cycles |volume=24 |issue=4 |article-number=2009GB003654 |bibcode=2010GBioC..24.4010B |doi=10.1029/2009GB003654 |s2cid=53062358 |bibcode-access=free |doi-access=free |s2cid-access=free}}</ref> The depth at which this occurs is known as the [[carbonate compensation depth]]. Ocean acidification will increase such dissolution and shallow the carbonate compensation depth on timescales of tens to hundreds of years.<ref name=":13"/> Zones of [[downwelling]] are being affected first.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sulpis |first1=Olivier |last2=Boudreau |first2=Bernard P. |last3=Mucci |first3=Alfonso |last4=Jenkins |first4=Chris |last5=Trossman |first5=David S. |last6=Arbic |first6=Brian K. |last7=Key |first7=Robert M. |date=13 November 2018 |title=Current CaCO3 dissolution at the seafloor caused by anthropogenic CO2 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=115 |issue=46 |pages=11700–11705 |bibcode=2018PNAS..11511700S |doi=10.1073/pnas.1804250115 |pmc=6243283 |pmid=30373837 |bibcode-access=free |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the North Pacific and North Atlantic, saturation states are also decreasing (the depth of saturation is getting more shallow).<ref name=":43"/>{{rp|396}} Ocean acidification is progressing in the open ocean as the {{CO2}} travels to deeper depth as a result of ocean mixing. In the open ocean, this causes carbonate compensation depths to become more shallow, meaning that dissolution of calcium carbonate will occur below those depths. In the North Pacific these carbonate saturations depths are shallowing at a rate of {{val|1|–|2|ul=m|upl=year}}.<ref name=":43"/>{{rp|396}}

It is expected that ocean acidification in the future will lead to a significant decrease in the burial of carbonate sediments for several centuries, and even the dissolution of existing carbonate sediments.<ref name="ridgwell07">{{cite journal |last1=Ridgwell |first1=A. |last2=Zondervan |first2=I. |last3=Hargreaves |first3=J. C. |last4=Bijma |first4=J. |last5=Lenton |first5=T. M. |year=2007 |title=Assessing the potential long-term increase of oceanic fossil fuel {{CO2}} uptake due to {{CO2}}-calcification feedback |journal=[[Biogeosciences]] |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=481–492 |bibcode=2007BGeo....4..481R |doi=10.5194/bg-4-481-2007 |bibcode-access=free |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Measured and estimated values==
===Present-day and recent history===
[[File:Co2 time series aloha 08-09-2023.jpg|thumb|right|Time series of atmospheric {{CO2}} at Mauna Loa (in parts per million volume, ppmv; red), surface ocean p{{CO2}} (μatm; green) and surface ocean pH (blue) at Ocean Station ALOHA in the subtropical North Pacific Ocean<ref>{{cite web |date=2012-09-07 |title=Atmospheric {{CO2}} and Ocean pH |url=https://cleanet.org/details/images/33568.html |access-date=2022-11-17 |website=CLEAN}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Quality of pH Measurements in the NODC Data Archives |url=https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/co2/story/Quality+of+pH+Measurements+in+the+NODC+Data+Archives |access-date=2023-12-18 |website=NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory}}</ref>]]
[[File: Estimated change in annual mean sea surface pH from 1770s-1990s (GLODAP).png|thumb|upright=1.3|Estimated change in seawater [[pH]] caused by [[anthropogenic impact]] on {{CO2|link=yes}} levels between the 1700s and the 1990s, from the [[Global Ocean Data Analysis Project]] (GLODAP) and the [[World Ocean Atlas]]|alt=World map showing the varying change to pH across different parts of different oceans]]Between 1950 and 2020, the average pH value of the ocean surface is estimated to have decreased from approximately 8.15 to 8.05.<ref name=role/> This represents an increase of around 26% in hydrogen ion concentration in the world's oceans (the pH scale is logarithmic, so a change of one in pH unit is equivalent to a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration).<ref name=":19">{{cite web |title=The pH Scale |url=https://www.whoi.edu/know-your-ocean/ocean-topics/how-the-ocean-works/ocean-chemistry/ocean-acidification/the-ph-scale/ |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution |language=en-US |archive-date=4 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004173658/https://www.whoi.edu/know-your-ocean/ocean-topics/how-the-ocean-works/ocean-chemistry/ocean-acidification/the-ph-scale/ |url-status=live}}</ref> For example, in the 15-year period 1995–2010 alone, acidity has increased 6 percent in the upper 100&nbsp;meters of the Pacific Ocean from Hawaii to Alaska.<ref name="2010aug_sciam">{{cite web |last1=Hardt |first1=Marah J. |last2=Safina |first2=Carl |date=9 August 2010 |title=How Acidification Threatens Oceans from the Inside Out |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=threatening-ocean-life |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101226161319/http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=threatening-ocean-life |archive-date=2010-12-26 |website=Scientific American}}</ref>

The [[IPCC Sixth Assessment Report]] in 2021 stated that "present-day surface pH values are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years and current rates of pH change are unprecedented since at least that time.<ref name=":82"/>{{rp|76}} The pH value of the ocean interior has declined over the last 20–30 years everywhere in the global ocean.<ref name=":82">Arias, P.A., N. Bellouin, E. Coppola, R.G. Jones, G. Krinner, J. Marotzke, V. Naik, M.D. Palmer, G.-K. Plattner, J. Rogelj, M. Rojas, J. Sillmann, T. Storelvmo, P.W. Thorne, B. Trewin, K. Achuta Rao, B. Adhikary, R.P. Allan, K. Armour, G. Bala, R. Barimalala, S. Berger, J.G. Canadell, C. Cassou, A. Cherchi, W. Collins, W.D. Collins, S.L. Connors, S. Corti, F. Cruz, F.J. Dentener, C. Dereczynski, A. Di Luca, A. Diongue Niang, F.J. Doblas-Reyes, A. Dosio, H. Douville, F. Engelbrecht, V. Eyring, E. Fischer, P. Forster, B. Fox-Kemper, J.S. Fuglestvedt, J.C. Fyfe, et al., 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_TS.pdf Technical Summary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220721021347/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_TS.pdf |date=21 July 2022}}. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210809131444/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ |date=9 August 2021}} [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US, pp. 33–144.</ref>{{rp|76}} The report also found that "pH in open ocean surface water has declined by about&nbsp;0.017 to 0.027 pH units per decade since the late 1980s".<ref name=":2">Canadell, J.G., P.M.S. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US, pp. 673–816.</ref>{{rp|716}}

The rate of decline differs by region. This is due to complex interactions between different types of forcing mechanisms:<ref name=":2"/>{{rp|716}} "In the tropical Pacific, its central and eastern upwelling zones exhibited a faster pH decline of minus 0.022 to minus 0.026 pH unit per decade." This is thought to be "due to increased [[upwelling]] of {{CO2}}-rich sub-surface waters in addition to anthropogenic {{CO2}} uptake".<ref name=":2"/>{{rp|716}} Some regions exhibited a slower acidification rate: a pH decline of minus 0.010 to minus 0.013 pH units per decade has been observed in warm pools in the western tropical Pacific.<ref name=":2"/>{{rp|716}}

The rate at which ocean acidification will occur may be influenced by the rate of [[sea surface temperature|surface ocean warming]], because warm waters will not absorb as much {{CO2}}.<ref name="humphreys20162">{{cite journal |last=Humphreys |first=M. P. |year=2016 |title=Climate sensitivity and the rate of ocean acidification: future impacts, and implications for experimental design |journal=ICES Journal of Marine Science |volume=74 |issue=4 |pages=934–940 |doi=10.1093/icesjms/fsw189 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Therefore, greater seawater warming could limit {{CO2}} absorption and lead to a smaller change in pH for a given increase in {{CO2}}.<ref name="humphreys20162"/> The difference in changes in temperature between basins is one of the main reasons for the differences in acidification rates in different localities.

Current rates of ocean acidification have been likened to the greenhouse event at the [[Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum|Paleocene–Eocene]] boundary (about 56&nbsp;million years ago), when surface ocean temperatures rose by {{val|5|–|6|ul=degC}}. In that event, surface ecosystems experienced a variety of impacts, but bottom-dwelling organisms in the deep ocean actually experienced a major extinction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McInerney |first1=Francesca A. |last2=Wing |first2=Scott L. |date=2011-05-30 |title=The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum: A Perturbation of Carbon Cycle, Climate, and Biosphere with Implications for the Future |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=489–516 |bibcode=2011AREPS..39..489M |doi=10.1146/annurev-earth-040610-133431}}</ref> Currently, the rate of carbon addition to the atmosphere-ocean system is about ten times the rate that occurred at the Paleocene–Eocene boundary.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Zeebe |first=Richard E. |date=2012-05-30 |title=History of Seawater Carbonate Chemistry, Atmospheric CO 2, and Ocean Acidification |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=141–165 |bibcode=2012AREPS..40..141Z |doi=10.1146/annurev-earth-042711-105521}}</ref>

Extensive observational systems are now in place or being built for monitoring seawater {{CO2}} chemistry and acidification for both the global open ocean and some coastal systems.<ref name=":14"/>

===Geologic past===
Ocean acidification has occurred previously in Earth's history.<ref name=":9"/> It happened during the [[Capitanian mass extinction event|Capitanian mass extinction]],<ref name="bond15">Bond, D.P.G., Wignall, P.B., Joachimski, M.M., Sun, Y., Savov, I., Grasby, S.E., Beauchamp, B., and Blomeier, D.P. 2015. [https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsa/gsabulletin/article/127/9-10/1411/126168/an-abrupt-extinction-in-the-middle-permian An abrupt extinction in the Middle Permian (Capitanian) of the Boreal Realm (Spitsbergen) and its link to anoxia and acidification] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230725183857/https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsa/gsabulletin/article/127/9-10/1411/126168/an-abrupt-extinction-in-the-middle-permian |date=25 July 2023}}. ''Geological Society of America Bulletin'', '''127''' (9–10): 1411–1421.</ref><ref name="6th extinction">{{cite news |last=Hand |first=Eric |date=16 April 2015 |title=Sixth extinction, rivaling that of the dinosaurs, should join the big five, scientists say |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/sixth-extinction-rivaling-dinosaurs-should-join-big-five-scientists-say |work=Science |archive-date=31 October 2023 |access-date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031132644/https://www.science.org/content/article/sixth-extinction-rivaling-dinosaurs-should-join-big-five-scientists-say |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="bbc15BerezowAlex">{{cite news |last=Berezow |first=Alex |date=21 April 2015 |title=New mass extinction event identified by geologists |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-32397220 |publisher=BBC |archive-date=31 October 2023 |access-date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031134235/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-32397220 |url-status=live}}</ref> at the [[Permian-Triassic extinction event|end-Permian extinction]],<ref name="ClarksonP-TAcid">{{cite journal |last1=Clarkson |first1=M. |last5=Lehrmann |first5=D. |last6=Yu |first6=M. |last7=Wei |first7=J. |year=2010 |title=Calcium isotope constraints on the end-Permian mass extinction |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of the [[Triassic–Jurassic extinction event|end-Triassic extinction]],<ref name=":20">{{cite journal |last=Hautmann |first=Michael |date=September 2004 |title=Effect of end-Triassic {{CO2}} maximum on carbonate sedimentation and marine mass extinction |journal=Facies |volume=50 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/s10347-004-0020-y |s2cid=130658467}}</ref><ref name="GreeneOceanAcidTriassic">{{cite journal |last1=Greene |first1=Sarah E. |last2=Martindale |first2=Rowan C. |last3=Ritterbush |first3=Kathleen A. |last4=Bottjer |first4=David J. |last5=Corsetti |first5=Frank A. |last6=Berelson |first6=William |volume=249 |issue=1 |pages=119–127 |doi=10.1127/0077-7749/2008/0249-0119 |bibcode=2008NJGPA.249..119H}}</ref> and during the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]].<ref name="PNAS-20191021"/>

Three of the big five mass extinction events in the geologic past were associated with a rapid increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide, probably due to [[volcanism]] and/or thermal dissociation of marine [[clathrate hydrate|gas hydrates]].<ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last1=Clapham |first1=Matthew E. |last2=Renne |first2=Paul R. |date=2019-05-30 |title=Flood Basalts and Mass Extinctions |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3q4714cg |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=275–303 |bibcode=2019AREPS..47..275C |doi=10.1146/annurev-earth-053018-060136 |s2cid=133715470 |archive-date=6 January 2024 |access-date=22 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240106050337/https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3q4714cg |url-status=live}}</ref> Elevated {{CO2}} levels impacted biodiversity.<ref name="Zachos2005">{{cite journal |last1=Zachos |first1=James C. |last2=Röhl |first2=Ursula |last3=Schellenberg |first3=Stephen A. |last4=Sluijs |first4=Appy |last5=Hodell |first5=David A. |last6=Kelly |first6=Daniel C. |last7=Thomas |first7=Ellen |last8=Nicolo |first8=Micah |last9=Raffi |first9=Isabella |last10=Lourens |first10=Lucas J. |last11=McCarren |first11=Heather |last12=Kroon |first12=Dick |date=10 June 2005 |title=Rapid Acidification of the Ocean During the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum |journal=Science |volume=308 |issue=5728 |pages=1611–1615 |bibcode=2005Sci...308.1611Z |doi=10.1126/science.1109004 |pmid=15947184 |s2cid=26909706 |hdl-access=free |hdl=1874/385806}}</ref> Decreased {{chem2|CaCO3}} saturation due to seawater uptake of volcanogenic {{CO2}} has been suggested as a possible kill mechanism during the marine mass extinction at the end of the [[Triassic]].<ref name=":20"/> The end-Triassic biotic crisis is still the most well-established example of a marine mass extinction due to ocean acidification, because (a) carbon isotope records suggest enhanced volcanic activity that decreased the carbonate sedimentation which reduced the carbonate compensation depth and the carbonate saturation state, and a marine extinction coincided precisely in the stratigraphic record,<ref name=":4"/><ref name="GreeneOceanAcidTriassic"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lindström |first1=Sofie |last2=van de Schootbrugge |first2=Bas |last3=Hansen |first3=Katrine H. |last4=Pedersen |first4=Gunver K. |last5=Alsen |first5=Peter |last6=Thibault |first6=Nicolas |last7=Dybkjær |first7=Karen |last8=Bjerrum |first8=Christian J. |last9=Nielsen |first9=Lars Henrik |date=July 2017 |title=A new correlation of Triassic–Jurassic boundary successions in NW Europe, Nevada and Peru, and the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province: A time-line for the end-Triassic mass extinction |journal=Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology |volume=478 |pages=80–102 |bibcode=2017PPP...478...80L |doi=10.1016/j.palaeo.2016.12.025 |s2cid=133353132 |hdl-access=free |hdl=1874/351998}}</ref> and (b) there was pronounced selectivity of the extinction against organisms with thick aragonitic skeletons,<ref name=":4"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hautmann |first1=M. |last2=Stiller |first2=F. |last3=Huawei |first3=C. |last4=Jingeng |first4=S. |date=1 October 2008 |title=Extinction-Recovery Pattern of Level-Bottom Faunas Across the Triassic-Jurassic Boundary in Tibet: Implications for Potential Killing Mechanisms |url=https://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/9775/10/Hautmann_Extinction_2008.pdf |journal=PALAIOS |volume=23 |issue=10 |pages=711–718 |bibcode=2008Palai..23..711H |doi=10.2110/palo.2008.p08-005r |s2cid=42675849}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last=Hautmann |first=Michael |title=eLS |date=2012-08-15 |article-number=a0001655.pub3 |chapter=Extinction: End-Triassic Mass Extinction |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |doi=10.1002/9780470015902.a0001655.pub3 |isbn=978-0-470-01617-6 |s2cid=130434497}}</ref> which is predicted from experimental studies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fine |first1=Maoz |last2=Tchernov |first2=Dan |date=30 March 2007 |title=Scleractinian Coral Species Survive and Recover from Decalcification |journal=Science |volume=315 |issue=5820 |page=1811 |bibcode=2007Sci...315.1811F |doi=10.1126/science.1137094 |pmid=17395821 |s2cid=28535145}}</ref> Ocean acidification has also been suggested as a one cause of the end-Permian mass extinction<ref name="PayneOceanAcidPermian"/><ref name="ClarksonP-TAcid"/> and the end-Cretaceous crisis.<ref name="PNAS-20191021"/> Overall, multiple climatic stressors, including ocean acidification, was likely the cause of geologic extinction events.<ref name=":8"/>

The most notable example of ocean acidification is the [[Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum]] (PETM), which occurred approximately 56&nbsp;million years ago when massive amounts of carbon entered the ocean and atmosphere, and led to the dissolution of carbonate sediments across many ocean basins.<ref name="Zachos2005"/> Relatively new geochemical methods of testing for pH in the past indicate the pH dropped 0.3 units across the PETM.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Penman |first1=Donald E. |last2=Hönisch |first2=Bärbel |last3=Zeebe |first3=Richard E. |last4=Thomas |first4=Ellen |last5=Zachos |first5=James C. |date=May 2014 |title=Rapid and sustained surface ocean acidification during the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum |url=https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8X92P2F/download |journal=Paleoceanography |volume=29 |issue=5 |pages=357–369 |bibcode=2014PalOc..29..357P |doi=10.1002/2014PA002621 |archive-date=31 October 2023 |access-date=22 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031132648/https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8X92P2F/download |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gutjahr |first1=Marcus |last2=Ridgwell |first2=Andy |last3=Sexton |first3=Philip F. |last4=Anagnostou |first4=Eleni |last5=Pearson |first5=Paul N. |last6=Pälike |first6=Heiko |last7=Norris |first7=Richard D. |last8=Thomas |first8=Ellen |last9=Foster |first9=Gavin L. |date=August 2017 |title=Very large release of mostly volcanic carbon during the Palaeocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum |journal=Nature |volume=548 |issue=7669 |pages=573–577 |bibcode=2017Natur.548..573G |doi=10.1038/nature23646 |pmc=5582631 |pmid=28858305}}</ref> One study that solves the marine carbonate system for saturation state shows that it may not change much over the PETM, suggesting the rate of carbon release at our best geological analogy was much slower than human-induced carbon emissions. However, stronger [[proxy (climate)|proxy]] methods to test for saturation state are needed to assess how much this pH change may have affected calcifying organisms.

==Predicted future values==
[[File:Oa-sami.jpg|thumb|upright|''In situ'' {{CO2}} concentration sensor (SAMI-{{CO2}}), attached to a Coral Reef Early Warning System station, utilized in conducting ocean acidification studies near coral reef areas (by [[NOAA]] ([[Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory|AOML]]))]]
[[File:Oa-buoy-enrique-reef.jpg|thumb|A moored autonomous {{CO2}} buoy used for measuring {{CO2}} concentration and ocean acidification studies ([[NOAA]] (by [[Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory|PMEL]]))]]
Importantly, the rate of change in ocean acidification is much higher than in the geological past. This faster change prevents organisms from gradually adapting, and prevents climate cycle feedbacks from kicking in to mitigate ocean acidification. Ocean acidification is now on a path to reach lower pH levels than at any other point in the last 300&nbsp;million years.<ref name="NYT-20191021">{{cite news |last=Joel |first=Lucas |date=21 October 2019 |title=The Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Acidified the Ocean in a Flash – The Chicxulub event was as damaging to life in the oceans as it was to creatures on land, a study shows. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/21/science/chicxulub-asteroid-ocean-acid.html |access-date=22 October 2019 |work=The New York Times |archive-date=24 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191024040435/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/21/science/chicxulub-asteroid-ocean-acid.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="PNAS-20191021">{{cite journal |last1=Henehan |first1=Michael J. |last2=Ridgwell |first2=Andy |last3=Thomas |first3=Ellen |last4=Zhang |first4=Shuang |last5=Alegret |first5=Laia |last6=Schmidt |first6=Daniela N. |last7=Rae |first7=James W. B. |last8=Witts |first8=James D. |last9=Landman |first9=Neil H. |last10=Greene |first10=Sarah E. |last11=Huber |first11=Brian T. |last12=Super |first12=James R. |last13=Planavsky |first13=Noah J. |last14=Hull |first14=Pincelli M. |date=5 November 2019 |title=Rapid ocean acidification and protracted Earth system recovery followed the end-Cretaceous Chicxulub impact |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=116 |issue=45 |pages=22500–22504 |bibcode=2019PNAS..11622500H |doi=10.1073/pnas.1905989116 |pmc=6842625 |pmid=31636204 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The rate of ocean acidification (i.e. the rate of change in pH value) is also estimated to be unprecedented over that same time scale.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Geological Record of Ocean Acidification |url=http://journalistsresource.org/studies/environment/climate-change/geological-record-ocean-acidification/ |access-date=14 March 2012 |work=The Journalist's Resource |archive-date=13 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131213075026/http://journalistsresource.org/studies/environment/climate-change/geological-record-ocean-acidification/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":9"/> These expected changes are considered unprecedented in the geological record.<ref name="yale_ridgwell_acidrate">{{cite web |title=An Ominous Warning on the Effects of Ocean Acidification by Carl Zimmer: Yale Environment 360 |url=http://e360.yale.edu/content/feature.msp?id=2241 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140216034313/http://e360.yale.edu/content/feature.msp?id=2241 |archive-date=16 February 2014 |access-date=2014-01-25 |publisher=e360.yale.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Newspapers |first=Les Blumenthal-McClatchy |date=2010-04-22 |title=Report: Ocean acidification rising at unprecedented rate |url=http://www.mcclatchydc.com/news/nation-world/national/article24580576.html |website=mcclatchydc |access-date=27 June 2017 |archive-date=19 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210619150318/https://www.mcclatchydc.com/news/nation-world/national/article24580576.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":10"/> In combination with other ocean [[biogeochemical]] changes, this drop in pH value could undermine the functioning of marine ecosystems and disrupt the provision of many goods and services associated with the ocean, beginning as early as 2100.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |last1=Mora |first1=Camilo |last2=Wei |first2=Chih-Lin |last3=Rollo |first3=Audrey |last4=Amaro |first4=Teresa |last5=Baco |first5=Amy R. |last6=Billett |first6=David |last7=Bopp |first7=Laurent |last8=Chen |first8=Qi |last9=Collier |first9=Mark |last10=Danovaro |first10=Roberto |last11=Gooday |first11=Andrew J. |last12=Grupe |first12=Benjamin M. |last13=Halloran |first13=Paul R. |last14=Ingels |first14=Jeroen |last15=Jones |first15=Daniel O. B. |date=2013-10-15 |editor-last=Mace |editor-first=Georgina M. |title=Biotic and Human Vulnerability to Projected Changes in Ocean Biogeochemistry over the 21st Century |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=11 |issue=10 |article-number=e1001682 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1001682 |pmc=3797030 |pmid=24143135 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The extent of further ocean chemistry changes, including ocean pH, will depend on [[climate change mitigation]] efforts taken by nations and their governments.<ref name=":82"/> Different scenarios of projected [[socioeconomics|socioeconomic]] global changes are modelled by using the [[Shared Socioeconomic Pathways]] (SSP) scenarios.

Under a [[Shared Socioeconomic Pathways|very high emission scenario (SSP5-8.5)]], model projections estimate that surface ocean pH could decrease by as much as 0.44 units by the end of this century, compared to the end of the 19th century.<ref>Lee, J.-Y., J. Marotzke, G. Bala, L. Cao, S. Corti, J.P. Dunne, F. Engelbrecht, E. Fischer, J.C. Fyfe, C. Jones, A. Maycock, J. Mutemi, O. Ndiaye, S. Panickal, and T. Zhou, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_Chapter04.pdf Chapter 4: Future Global Climate: Scenario-Based Projections and Near- Term Information] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221109133340/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_Chapter04.pdf |date=9 November 2022}}. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_FullReport.pdf Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018055338/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_FullReport.pdf |date=18 October 2022}} [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US, pp. 553–672.</ref>{{rp|608}} This would mean a pH as low as about 7.7, and represents a further increase in H+ concentrations of two to four times beyond the increase to date.

[[File:Fis01026 (27555118153).jpg|thumb|Unhealthy pteropod showing effects of ocean acidification including ragged, dissolving shell ridges on upper surface, a cloudy shell in lower right quadrant, and severe abrasions and weak spots at 6:30 position on lower whorl of shell (source: [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|NOAA]])]]

===Complexity of research findings===
The full ecological consequences of the changes in calcification due to ocean acidification are complex but it appears likely that many calcifying species will be adversely affected by ocean acidification.<ref name=":14"/><ref name=":43"/>{{rp|413}} Increasing ocean acidification makes it more difficult for shell-accreting organisms to access carbonate ions, essential for the production of their hard exoskeletal shell.<ref name=":11">{{cite web |title=PMEL {{CO2}} – Carbon Dioxide Program |url=https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/co2 |access-date=2021-09-06 |website=NOAA Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory |archive-date=5 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231205124717/https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/co2 |url-status=live}}</ref> Oceanic [[calcification|calcifying]] organism span the [[food chain]] from [[autotroph]]s to [[heterotroph]]s and include organisms such as [[coccolithophore]]s, [[coral]]s, [[foraminifera]], [[echinoderm]]s, [[crustacea]]ns, and [[Mollusca|molluscs]].<ref name=":3"/><ref name=":0">National Research Council. ''[http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12877&page=R1 Overview of Climate Changes and Illustrative Impacts. Climate Stabilization Targets: Emissions, Concentrations, and Impacts over Decades to Millennia]'' {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906174354/http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12877&page=R1 |date=6 September 2015}}. Washington, D.C.: The National Academies Press, 2011. 1. Print.</ref>

Overall, all marine ecosystems on Earth will be exposed to changes in acidification and several other ocean biogeochemical changes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fairchild |first1=William |last2=Hales |first2=Burke |date=14 January 2021 |title=High-Resolution Carbonate System Dynamics of Netarts Bay, OR From 2014 to 2019 |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=7 |article-number=590236 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2020.590236 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021FrMaS...790236F}}</ref> Ocean acidification may force some organisms to reallocate resources away from productive endpoints in order to maintain calcification.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=Hannah L. |last2=Spicer |first2=John I. |last3=Widdicombe |first3=Stephen |year=2008 |title=Ocean acidification may increase calcification rates, but at a cost |journal=[[Proceedings of the Royal Society B]] |volume=275 |issue=1644 |pages=1767–1773 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2008.0343 |pmc=2587798 |pmid=18460426}}</ref> For example, the oyster ''[[Pacific oyster|Magallana gigas]]'' is recognized to experience metabolic changes alongside altered [[calcification]] rates due to energetic tradeoffs resulting from pH imbalances.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal |last1=Ducker |first1=James |last2=Falkenberg |first2=Laura J. |date=12 November 2020 |title=How the Pacific Oyster Responds to Ocean Acidification: Development and Application of a Meta-Analysis Based Adverse Outcome Pathway |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=7 |article-number=597441 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2020.597441 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020FrMaS...797441D}}</ref>

Under normal conditions, calcite and aragonite are stable in surface waters since the carbonate ions are [[supersaturation|supersaturated]] with respect to seawater. However, as ocean pH falls, the concentration of carbonate ions also decreases. Calcium carbonate thus becomes undersaturated, and structures made of calcium carbonate are vulnerable to calcification stress and dissolution.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Spalding |first1=Christopher |last2=Finnegan |first2=Seth |last3=Fischer |first3=Woodward W. |date=May 2017 |title=Energetic costs of calcification under ocean acidification |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/77249/ |journal=Global Biogeochemical Cycles |volume=31 |issue=5 |pages=866–877 |bibcode=2017GBioC..31..866S |doi=10.1002/2016GB005597 |s2cid=133783884 |archive-date=18 September 2020 |access-date=22 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918023536/https://authors.library.caltech.edu/77249/}}</ref> In particular, studies show that corals,<ref name="ocean">{{cite news |date=14 November 2013 |title=Ocean Acidification Summary for Policymakers |url=http://www.igbp.net/publications/summariesforpolicymakers/summariesforpolicymakers/oceanacidificationsummaryforpolicymakers2013.5.30566fc6142425d6c9111f4.html |publisher=IGBP |archive-date=23 July 2019 |access-date=2 January 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190723171830/http://www.igbp.net/publications/summariesforpolicymakers/summariesforpolicymakers/oceanacidificationsummaryforpolicymakers2013.5.30566fc6142425d6c9111f4.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{cite web |date=2019-09-25 |title=Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate – Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate |url=https://www.ipcc.ch/srocc/home/ |access-date=2019-11-12 |website=IPCC |archive-date=4 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204193600/https://www.ipcc.ch/srocc/home/ |url-status=live}}</ref> coccolithophores,<ref name=":0"/><ref name="Carstensen2019"/><ref name="gatt98">{{cite journal |last=Gattuso |first=J |date=July 1998 |title=Effect of calcium carbonate saturation of seawater on coral calcification |journal=Global and Planetary Change |volume=18 |issue=1–2 |pages=37–46 |bibcode=1998GPC....18...37G |doi=10.1016/S0921-8181(98)00035-6}}</ref> coralline algae,<ref name="gatt99">{{cite journal |last1=Gattuso |first1=Jean-Pierre |last2=Allemand |first2=Denis |last3=Frankignoulle |first3=Michel |date=February 1999 |title=Photosynthesis and Calcification at Cellular, Organismal and Community Levels in Coral Reefs: A Review on Interactions and Control by Carbonate Chemistry |journal=American Zoologist |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=160–183 |doi=10.1093/icb/39.1.160}}</ref> foraminifera,<ref name="lan05">{{cite journal |last1=Langdon |first1=C. |last2=Atkinson |first2=M. J. |year=2005 |title=Effect of elevated p{{CO2}} on photosynthesis and calcification of corals and interactions with seasonal change in temperature/irradiance and nutrient enrichment |journal=[[Journal of Geophysical Research]] |volume=110 |issue=C09S07 |pages=C09S07 |doi=10.1029/2004JC002576 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2005JGRC..110.9S07L}}</ref> shellfish and [[Pteropoda|pteropods]]<ref name="rieb00">{{cite journal |last1=Riebesell |first1=Ulf |last2=Zondervan |first2=Ingrid |last3=Rost |first3=Björn |last4=Tortell |first4=Philippe D. |last5=Zeebe |first5=Richard E. |last6=Morel |first6=François M. M. |date=September 2000 |title=Reduced calcification of marine plankton in response to increased atmospheric {{CO2}} |url=https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/3784/1/Rie2000a.pdf |journal=Nature |volume=407 |issue=6802 |pages=364–367 |bibcode=2000Natur.407..364R |doi=10.1038/35030078 |pmid=11014189 |s2cid=4426501 |archive-date=25 August 2020 |access-date=19 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200825233008/https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/3784/1/Rie2000a.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> experience reduced calcification or enhanced dissolution when exposed to elevated {{CO2}}. Even with active [[marine conservation]] practices it may be impossible to bring back many previous shellfish populations.<ref name="gaz07">{{cite journal |last1=Gazeau |first1=Frédéric |last2=Quiblier |first2=Christophe |last3=Jansen |first3=Jeroen M. |last4=Gattuso |first4=Jean-Pierre |last5=Middelburg |first5=Jack J. |last6=Heip |first6=Carlo H. R. |date=6 April 2007 |title=Impact of elevated CO 2 on shellfish calcification |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03334206/file/2006GL028554.pdf |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=34 |issue=7 |pages=L07603 |bibcode=2007GeoRL..34.7603G |doi=10.1029/2006GL028554 |s2cid=130190489 |hdl-access=free |hdl=20.500.11755/a8941c6a-6d0b-43d5-ba0d-157a7aa05668 |archive-date=27 May 2022 |access-date=22 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220527235730/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03334206/file/2006GL028554.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

Some studies have found different responses to ocean acidification, with coccolithophore calcification and photosynthesis both increasing under elevated atmospheric [[pCO2|p{{CO2}}]],<ref name="Iglesias2008">{{cite journal |last1=Iglesias-Rodriguez |first1=M.D. |last2=Halloran, P.R. |last3=Rickaby, R.E.M. |last4=Hall, I.R. |last5=Colmenero-Hidalgo, E. |last6=Gittins, J.R. |last7=Green, D.R.H. |last8=Tyrrell, T. |last9=Gibbs, S.J. |last10=von Dassow, P. |last11=Rehm, E. |last12=Armbrust, E.V. |last13=Boessenkool, K.P. |year=2008 |title=Phytoplankton Calcification in a High-{{CO2}} World |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=320 |issue=5874 |pages=336–340 |bibcode=2008Sci...320..336I |doi=10.1126/science.1154122 |pmid=18420926 |s2cid=206511068}}</ref> and an equal decline in [[primary production]] and calcification in response to elevated {{CO2}},<ref name="sciandra03">{{cite journal |last1=Sciandra |first1=Antoine |last2=Harlay |first2=Jérome |last3=Lefèvre |first3=Dominique |last4=Lemée |first4=Rodolphe |last5=Rimmelin |first5=Peguy |last6=Denis |first6=Michel |last7=Gattuso |first7=Jean-Pierre |date=17 October 2003 |title=Response of coccolithophorid Emiliania huxleyi to elevated partial pressure of {{CO2}} under nitrogen limitation |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |volume=261 |pages=111–122 |bibcode=2003MEPS..261..111S |doi=10.3354/meps261111 |doi-access=free}}</ref> or the direction of the response varying between species.<ref name="langer06">{{cite journal |last1=Langer |first1=Gerald |last2=Geisen |first2=Markus |last3=Baumann |first3=Karl-Heinz |last4=Kläs |first4=Jessica |last5=Riebesell |first5=Ulf |last6=Thoms |first6=Silke |last7=Young |first7=Jeremy R. |date=September 2006 |title=Species-specific responses of calcifying algae to changing seawater carbonate chemistry |url=https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/14731/1/Lan2006e.pdf |journal=Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems |volume=7 |issue=9 |article-number=2005GC001227 |bibcode=2006GGG.....7.9006L |doi=10.1029/2005GC001227 |s2cid=14774230 |archive-date=22 December 2023 |access-date=20 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231222150307/https://epic.awi.de/id/eprint/14731/1/Lan2006e.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

Similarly, the sea star, [[Pisaster ochraceus]], shows enhanced growth in waters with increased acidity.<ref name="Turley 278–2862">{{cite journal |last1=Turley |first1=Carol |last2=Gattuso |first2=Jean-Pierre |date=July 2012 |title=Future biological and ecosystem impacts of ocean acidification and their socioeconomic-policy implications |journal=Current Opinion in Environmental Sustainability |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=278–286 |bibcode=2012COES....4..278T |doi=10.1016/j.cosust.2012.05.007 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Reduced calcification from ocean acidification&nbsp;may affect the ocean's biologically driven sequestration of [[carbon]] from the atmosphere to the ocean interior and [[seafloor sediment]], weakening the so-called [[biological pump]].<ref name="PNAS-20191021"/> Seawater acidification could also reduce the size of Antarctic phytoplankton, making them less effective at storing carbon.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Petrou |first1=Katherina |last2=Nielsen |first2=Daniel |date=2019-08-27 |title=Acid oceans are shrinking plankton, fueling faster climate change |url=https://phys.org/news/2019-08-acid-oceans-plankton-fueling-faster.html |access-date=2019-11-12 |website=phys.org |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031132927/https://phys.org/news/2019-08-acid-oceans-plankton-fueling-faster.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Such changes are being increasingly studied and synthesized through the use of physiological frameworks, including the [[Adverse outcome pathway|Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP)]] framework.<ref name=":6"/>
[[File:Coccolithus pelagicus.jpg|thumb|''Coccolithus pelagicus'', a species of [[coccolithophore]] sampled from the North Atlantic Ocean]][[Life-cycle assessment|Life-cycle assessment (LCA)]] [[Life-cycle assessment|and life-cycle impact assessments (LCIA)]] methods can be used to estimate potential marine biodiversity damage driven by emissions through the ocean acidification pathway. These methods combine modeled changes in seawater chemistry with data on the sensitivity of marine organisms. A 2025 study developed spatially differentiated characterization factors for carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane emissions across 232 coastal marine ecoregions and 18 open-ocean fishing areas. The resulting estimates showed substantial geographical variation in potential biodiversity impacts<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Sedona R. |last2=Stadler |first2=Konstantin |last3=Verones |first3=Francesca |date=2025-10-28 |title=From Global Emissions to Local Impacts: Spatially Explicit Modeling of Ocean Acidification in Life Cycle Assessment |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |language=en |volume=59 |issue=42 |pages=22508–22517 |doi=10.1021/acs.est.5c02069 |issn=0013-936X |pmc=12573785 |pmid=41100707 |bibcode=2025EnST...5922508A }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Scherer |first1=Laura |last2=Gürdal |first2=İrem |last3=van Bodegom |first3=Peter M. |date=December 2022 |title=Characterization factors for ocean acidification impacts on marine biodiversity |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jiec.13274 |journal=Journal of Industrial Ecology |language=en |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=2069–2079 |doi=10.1111/jiec.13274 |bibcode=2022JInEc..26.2069S |issn=1088-1980}}</ref>.

===Coccolithophores===
{{Further|Coccolithophore}}
A coccolithophore is a [[unicellular organism|unicellular]], [[eukaryotic]] [[phytoplankton]] ([[alga]]). Understanding calcification changes in coccolithophores may be particularly important because a decline in the coccolithophores may have secondary effects on climate: it could contribute to global warming by decreasing the Earth's [[albedo]] via their effects on oceanic cloud cover.<ref name="Stony2010">{{cite press release |title=Acidification of Oceans May Contribute To Global Declines of Shellfish, Study By Stony Brook Scientists Concludes |date=27 September 2010 |publisher=School of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences at Stony Brook University |url=http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Acidification_Of_Oceans_May_Contribute_To_Global_Declines_Of_Shellfish_Study_By_Stony_Brook_Scientists_Concludes.shtml |access-date=4 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903222130/http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Acidification_Of_Oceans_May_Contribute_To_Global_Declines_Of_Shellfish_Study_By_Stony_Brook_Scientists_Concludes.shtml |archive-date=3 September 2012}}</ref> A study in 2008 examined a [[sedimentology|sediment core]] from the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic]] and found that the species composition of coccolithophorids remained unchanged over the past 224 years (1780 to 2004). But the average coccolith mass had increased by 40% during the same period.<ref name="Iglesias2008"/>

===Corals===
{{Further|Coral|Coral reef}}
Warm water corals are clearly in decline, with losses of 50% over the last 30–50 years due to multiple threats from ocean warming, ocean acidification, [[marine pollution|pollution]], and physical damage from activities such as fishing, and these pressures are expected to intensify.<ref name=":32">{{cite journal |last1=Hoegh-Guldberg |first1=Ove |last2=Poloczanska |first2=Elvira S. |last3=Skirving |first3=William |last4=Dove |first4=Sophie |date=2017 |title=Coral Reef Ecosystems under Climate Change and Ocean Acidification |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=4 |article-number=158 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2017.00158 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2017FrMaS...4..158H}}</ref><ref name=":43"/>{{rp|416}}

The fluid in the internal compartments (the coelenteron) where corals grow their [[exoskeleton]] is also extremely important for calcification growth. When the saturation state of aragonite in the external seawater is at ambient levels, the corals will grow their aragonite crystals rapidly in their internal compartments, hence their exoskeleton grows rapidly. If the saturation state of aragonite in the external seawater is lower than the ambient level, the corals have to work harder to maintain the right balance in the internal compartment. When that happens, the process of growing the crystals slows down, and this slows down the rate of how much their exoskeleton is growing. Depending on the aragonite saturation state&nbsp;in the surrounding water, the corals may halt growth because pumping aragonite&nbsp;into the internal compartment will not be energetically favorable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=A. |last2=Holcomb |first2=M. |year=2009 |title=Why Corals Care About Ocean Acidification: Uncovering the Mechanism |journal=Oceanography |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=118–127 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2009.102 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2009Ocgpy..22d.118C}}</ref> Under the current progression of carbon emissions, around 70% of North Atlantic cold-water corals will be living in corrosive waters by 2050–60.<ref name="Perez2018">{{cite journal |last1=Pérez |first1=F. |last2=Fontela |first2=M. |last3=García-Ibañez |first3=M. |last4=Mercier |first4=H. |last5=Velo |first5=A. |last6=Lherminier |first6=P. |last7=Zunino |first7=P. |last8=de la Paz |first8=M. |last9=Alonso |first9=F. |last10=Guallart |first10=E. |last11=Padín |first11=T. |date=22 February 2018 |title=Meridional overturning circulation conveys fast acidification to the deep Atlantic Ocean |url=https://archimer.ifremer.fr/doc/00426/53783/ |journal=Nature |volume=554 |issue=7693 |pages=515–518 |bibcode=2018Natur.554..515P |doi=10.1038/nature25493 |pmid=29433125 |s2cid=3497477 |hdl=10261/162241 |archive-date=22 March 2023 |access-date=20 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322161130/https://archimer.ifremer.fr/doc/00426/53783/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Acidified conditions primarily reduce the coral's capacity to build dense exoskeletons, rather than affecting the linear extension of the exoskeleton. The density of some species of corals could be reduced by over 20% by the end of this century.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mollica |first1=Nathaniel R. |last2=Guo |first2=Weifu |last3=Cohen |first3=Anne L. |last4=Huang |first4=Kuo-Fang |last5=Foster |first5=Gavin L. |last6=Donald |first6=Hannah K. |last7=Solow |first7=Andrew R. |date=20 February 2018 |title=Ocean acidification affects coral growth by reducing skeletal density |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=115 |issue=8 |pages=1754–1759 |bibcode=2018PNAS..115.1754M |doi=10.1073/pnas.1712806115 |pmc=5828584 |pmid=29378969 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

An ''in situ'' experiment, conducted on a 400 m2 patch of the [[Great Barrier Reef]], to decrease seawater {{CO2}} level (raise pH) to near the preindustrial value showed a 7% increase in net calcification.<ref name="Albright2016">{{cite journal |last1=Albright |first1=R. |last2=Caldeira |first2=L. |last3=Hosfelt |first3=J. |last4=Kwiatkowski |first4=L. |last5=Maclaren |first5=J. K. |last6=Mason |first6=B. M. |last7=Nebuchina |first7=Y. |last8=Ninokawa |first8=A. |last9=Pongratz |first9=J. |last10=Ricke |first10=K. L. |last11=Rivlin |first11=T. |last12=Schneider |first12=K. |last13=Sesboüé |first13=M. |last14=Shamberger |first14=K. |last15=Silverman |first15=J. |date=24 February 2016 |title=Reversal of ocean acidification enhances net coral reef calcification |journal=Nature |volume=531 |issue=7594 |pages=362–365 |bibcode=2016Natur.531..362A |doi=10.1038/nature17155 |pmid=26909578 |s2cid=205247928 |last16=Wolfe |first16=K. |last17=Zhu |first17=K. |last18=Caldeira |first18=K.}}</ref> A similar experiment to raise in situ seawater {{CO2}} level (lower pH) to a level expected soon after the 2050 found that net calcification decreased 34%.<ref name="Albright2018">{{cite journal |last1=Albright |first1=R. |last2=Takeshita |first2=T. |last3=Koweek |first3=D. A. |last4=Ninokawa |first4=A. |last5=Wolfe |first5=K. |last6=Rivlin |first6=T. |last7=Nebuchina |first7=Y. |last8=Young |first8=J. |last9=Caldeira |first9=K. |date=14 March 2018 |title=Carbon dioxide addition to coral reef waters suppresses net community calcification |journal=Nature |volume=555 |issue=7697 |pages=516–519 |bibcode=2018Natur.555..516A |doi=10.1038/nature25968 |pmid=29539634 |s2cid=3935534}}</ref>

However, a field study of the coral reef in [[Queensland]] and [[Western Australia]] from 2007 to 2012 found that corals are more resistant to the environmental pH changes than previously thought, due to internal [[homeostasis]] regulation; this makes thermal change ([[marine heatwave]]s), which leads to [[coral bleaching]], rather than acidification, the main factor for coral reef vulnerability due to climate change.<ref name="MUNDAY"/>

====Studies at carbon dioxide seep sites====
In some places carbon dioxide bubbles out from the sea floor, locally changing the pH and other aspects of the chemistry of the seawater. Studies of these carbon dioxide seeps have documented a variety of responses by different organisms.<ref name="pmid18536730">{{cite journal |last1=Hall-Spencer |first1=Jason M. |last2=Rodolfo-Metalpa |first2=Riccardo |last3=Martin |first3=Sophie |last4=Ransome |first4=Emma |last5=Fine |first5=Maoz |last6=Turner |first6=Suzanne M. |last7=Rowley |first7=Sonia J. |last8=Tedesco |first8=Dario |last9=Buia |first9=Maria-Cristina |date=July 2008 |title=Volcanic carbon dioxide vents show ecosystem effects of ocean acidification |journal=Nature |volume=454 |issue=7200 |pages=96–99 |bibcode=2008Natur.454...96H |doi=10.1038/nature07051 |pmid=18536730 |s2cid=9375062 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10026.1/1345}}</ref> Coral reef communities located near carbon dioxide seeps are of particular interest because of the sensitivity of some corals species to acidification. In Papua New Guinea, declining pH caused by carbon dioxide seeps is associated with declines in coral species diversity.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Fabricius |first=Katharina |date=2011 |title=Losers and winners in coral reefs acclimatized to elevated carbon dioxide concentrations |journal=Nature Climate Change |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=165–169 |bibcode=2011NatCC...1..165F |doi=10.1038/nclimate1122 |s2cid=85749253}}</ref> However, in [[Palau]] carbon dioxide seeps are not associated with reduced species diversity of corals, although [[bioerosion]] of coral skeletons is much higher at low pH sites.

===Pteropods and brittle stars===
[[Pteropoda|Pteropods]] and [[brittle star]]s both form the base of the Arctic [[food web]]s and are both seriously damaged from acidification. Pteropods shells dissolve with increasing acidification and the brittle stars lose muscle mass when re-growing [[appendage]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Effects of Ocean Acidification on Marine Species & Ecosystems |url=http://oceana.org/en/our-work/climate-energy/ocean-acidification/learn-act/effects-of-ocean-acidification-on-marine-species-ecosystems |access-date=13 October 2013 |website=Report |publisher=OCEANA |archive-date=25 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141225091214/http://oceana.org/en/our-work/climate-energy/ocean-acidification/learn-act/effects-of-ocean-acidification-on-marine-species-ecosystems}}</ref> For pteropods to create shells they require aragonite which is produced through carbonate ions and dissolved calcium and strontium. Pteropods are severely affected because increasing acidification levels have steadily decreased the amount of water supersaturated with carbonate.<ref name="biogeosciences">{{cite journal |last1=Lischka |first1=S. |last2=Büdenbender |first2=J. |last3=Boxhammer |first3=T. |last4=Riebesell |first4=U. |date=15 April 2011 |title=Impact of ocean acidification and elevated temperatures on early juveniles of the polar shelled pteropod ''Limacina helicina'': mortality, shell degradation, and shell growth |journal=Biogeosciences |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=919–932 |bibcode=2011BGeo....8..919L |doi=10.5194/bg-8-919-2011 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The degradation of organic matter in Arctic waters has amplified ocean acidification;
