some Arctic waters are already undersaturated with respect to aragonite.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mathis |first1=Jeremy T. |last2=Cross |first2=Jessica N. |last3=Evans |first3=Wiley |last4=Doney |first4=Scott C. |date=2015 |title=Ocean Acidification in the Surface Waters of the Pacific-Arctic Boundary Regions |journal=Oceanography |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=122–135 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2015.36 |jstor=24861875 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2015Ocgpy..25b.122M}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Semiletov |first1=Igor |last2=Pipko |first2=Irina |last3=Gustafsson |first3=Örjan |last4=Anderson |first4=Leif G. |last5=Sergienko |first5=Valentin |last6=Pugach |first6=Svetlana |last7=Dudarev |first7=Oleg |last8=Charkin |first8=Alexander |last9=Gukov |first9=Alexander |last10=Bröder |first10=Lisa |last11=Andersson |first11=August |last12=Spivak |first12=Eduard |last13=Shakhova |first13=Natalia |date=2016 |title=Acidification of East Siberian Arctic Shelf waters through addition of freshwater and terrestrial carbon |journal=Nature Geoscience |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=361–365 |bibcode=2016NatGe...9..361S |doi=10.1038/ngeo2695 |s2cid=131084581}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Terhaar |first1=Jens |last2=Kwiatkowski |first2=Lester |last3=Bopp |first3=Laurent |date=2020-06-18 |title=Emergent constraint on Arctic Ocean acidification in the twenty-first century |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02884111/file/Terhaar_Nature_2020_preprint.pdf |journal=Nature |volume=582 |issue=7812 |pages=379–383 |bibcode=2020Natur.582..379T |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2360-3 |pmid=32555488 |s2cid=219729997 |archive-date=17 November 2022 |access-date=22 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221117200418/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02884111/file/Terhaar_Nature_2020_preprint.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

The brittle star's eggs die within a few days when exposed to expected conditions resulting from Arctic acidification.<ref name=":02">{{cite web |title=Comprehensive study of Arctic Ocean acidification |url=http://www.cicero.uio.no/webnews/index_e.aspx?id=11909 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131210231159/http://www.cicero.uio.no/webnews/index_e.aspx?id=11909 |archive-date=10 December 2013 |access-date=14 November 2013 |website=Study |publisher=CICERO}}</ref> Similarly, when exposed in experiments to pH reduced by 0.2 to 0.4, larvae of a temperate [[brittle star]], a relative of the common [[sea star]], fewer than 0.1 percent survived more than eight days.<ref name=":3"/>

==Other impacts on ecosystems==
[[File:Changes in aragonite saturation of the world's oceans, 1880-2012 (US EPA).png|thumb|upright=1.5|This map shows changes in the aragonite saturation level of ocean surface waters between the 1880s and 2006–2015. Aragonite is a form of calcium carbonate that many marine animals use to build their skeletons and shells. The lower the saturation level, the more difficult it is for organisms to build and maintain their skeletons and shells. A negative change represents a decrease in saturation.<ref>{{cite web |last=Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution |date=August 2016 |title=Changes in Aragonite Saturation of the World's Oceans, 1880–2015 |url=https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-acidity |website=epa.gov |access-date=9 February 2019 |archive-date=15 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230215162813/https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/climate-change-indicators-ocean-acidity |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

===Other biological impacts===
Aside from the slowing and/or reversal of calcification, organisms may suffer other adverse effects, either indirectly through negative impacts on food resources, or directly as reproductive or physiological effects.<ref name="raven05"/> For example, the elevated oceanic levels of {{CO2}} may produce {{CO2}}-induced acidification of body fluids, known as [[hypercapnia]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Onthank |first1=Kirt |last2=Trueblood |first2=Lloyd |last3=Schrock-Duff |first3=Taylir |last4=Kore |first4=Lydia |date=2021 |title=Impact of short- and long-term exposure to elevated seawater p{{CO2}} on metabolic rate and hypoxia tolerance in Octopus rubescens [Dataset] |journal=Physiological and Biochemical Zoology |publisher=Dryad Data Platform |volume=94 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.5061/dryad.pg4f4qrj8}}</ref>
Increasing acidity has been observed to reduce metabolic rates in [[jumbo squid]]<ref name="Rosa">{{cite journal |last1=Rosa |first1=R. |last2=Seibel |first2=B. |year=2008 |title=Synergistic effects of climate-related variables suggest future physiological impairment in a top oceanic predator |journal=PNAS |volume=105 |issue=52 |pages=20776–20780 |bibcode=2008PNAS..10520776R |doi=10.1073/pnas.0806886105 |pmc=2634909 |pmid=19075232 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and depress the immune responses of blue mussels.<ref name="Bibby">{{cite journal |last1=Bibby |first1=R |last2=Widdicombe |first2=S |last3=Parry |first3=H |last4=Spicer |first4=J |last5=Pipe |first5=R |date=27 March 2008 |title=Effects of ocean acidification on the immune response of the blue mussel Mytilus edulis |journal=Aquatic Biology |volume=2 |pages=67–74 |doi=10.3354/ab00037 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2008AquaB...2...67B}}</ref>
[[Atlantic longfin squid]] eggs took longer to hatch in acidified water, and the squid's [[statocyst|statolith]] was smaller and malformed in animals placed in sea water with a lower pH.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kwok |first=Roberta |date=4 June 2013 |title=Ocean acidification could make squid develop abnormally |url=http://conservationmagazine.org/2013/06/stunted-growth/ |access-date=2013-08-24 |publisher=University of Washington |archive-date=30 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141030031542/http://conservationmagazine.org/2013/06/stunted-growth/ |url-status=live}}</ref> However, these studies are ongoing and there is not yet a full understanding of these processes in marine organisms or [[ecosystem]]s.<ref name="Ocean Acidification and Krill">{{cite news |year=2008 |title=Swiss marine researcher moving in for the krill |url=http://www.theaustralian.news.com.au/story/0,25197,24392216-27703,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081211233233/http://www.theaustralian.news.com.au/story/0,25197,24392216-27703,00.html |archive-date=11 December 2008 |access-date=28 September 2008 |work=The Australian}}</ref>

====Acoustic properties====
Another potential route to ecosystem impacts is through [[bioacoustics]]. This may occur as ocean acidification can alter the [[acoustics|acoustic]] properties of seawater, allowing sound to propagate further, and increasing ocean noise.<ref name="Hester">{{cite journal |last1=Hester |first1=Keith C. |last2=Peltzer |first2=Edward T. |last3=Kirkwood |first3=William J. |last4=Brewer |first4=Peter G. |date=1 October 2008 |title=Unanticipated consequences of ocean acidification: A noisier ocean at lower pH |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=35 |issue=19 |pages=L19601 |bibcode=2008GeoRL..3519601H |doi=10.1029/2008GL034913 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This impacts all animals that use sound for [[animal echolocation|echolocation]] or [[whale song|communication]].<ref name="npr-threat">[https://www.npr.org/templates/transcript/transcript.php?storyId=111807469 Acid In The Oceans: A Growing Threat To Sea Life] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180512043714/https://www.npr.org/templates/transcript/transcript.php?storyId=111807469 |date=12 May 2018}} by Richard Harris. All Things Considered, 12 August 2009.</ref>

====Algae and seagrasses====
{{Further|Eutrophication}}
Another possible effect would be an increase in [[harmful algal bloom]] events, which could contribute to the accumulation of toxins ([[domoic acid]], [[brevetoxin]], [[saxitoxin]]) in small organisms such as [[anchovies]] and [[shellfish]], in turn increasing occurrences of [[amnesic shellfish poisoning]], [[neurotoxic shellfish poisoning]], and [[paralytic shellfish poisoning]].<ref name="Ocean Acidification Promotes Disruptive and Harmful Algal Blooms on Our Coasts">{{cite web |year=2014 |title=Ocean Acidification Promotes Disruptive and Harmful Algal Blooms on Our Coasts |url=http://coastalscience.noaa.gov/news/climate/ocean-acidification-promotes-disruptive-and-harmful-algal-blooms-on-our-coasts/ |access-date=3 June 2015 |archive-date=26 June 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626012257/http://coastalscience.noaa.gov/news/climate/ocean-acidification-promotes-disruptive-and-harmful-algal-blooms-on-our-coasts/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Although algal blooms can be harmful, other beneficial photosynthetic organisms may benefit from increased levels of carbon dioxide. Most importantly, seagrasses will benefit.<ref name="Turley 278–2862"/> Research found that as seagrasses increased their photosynthetic activity, calcifying algae's calcification rates rose, likely because localized photosynthetic activity absorbed carbon dioxide and elevated local pH.<ref name="Turley 278–2862"/>

====Fish larvae====

Ocean acidification can also impact marine [[fish larvae]]. It internally affects their olfactory systems, which is a crucial part of their early development. [[Orange clownfish]] larvae mostly live on oceanic reefs that are surrounded by vegetative islands{{clarify|date=October 2023}}.<ref name="MUNDAY">{{cite journal |last=Munday |first=Philip L. |year=2009 |title=Ocean Acidification Impairs Olfactory Discrimination and Homing Ability of a Marine Fish |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=6 |pages=1848–52 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.1848M |doi=10.1073/pnas.0809996106 |pmc=2644126 |pmid=19188596 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Larvae are known to use their sense of smell to detect the differences between reefs surrounded by vegetative islands and reefs not surrounded by vegetative islands.<ref name="MUNDAY"/> Clownfish larvae need to be able to distinguish between these two destinations to find a suitable area for their growth. Another use for marine fish olfactory systems is to distinguish between their parents and other adult fish, in order to avoid inbreeding.

In an experimental aquarium facility, clownfish were sustained in non-manipulated seawater with pH 8.15&nbsp;± 0.07, which is similar to our current ocean's pH.<ref name="MUNDAY"/> To test for effects of different pH levels, the seawater was modified to two other pH levels, which corresponded with climate change models that predict future atmospheric {{CO2}} levels.<ref name="MUNDAY"/> In the year 2100 the model projects possible {{CO2}} levels of 1,000&nbsp;ppm, which correlates with the pH of 7.8&nbsp;± 0.05.

This experiment showed that when larvae are exposed to a pH of 7.8&nbsp;± 0.05 their reaction to environmental cues differs drastically from their reaction to cues at pH equal to current ocean levels.<ref name="MUNDAY"/> At pH 7.6&nbsp;± 0.05 larvae had no reaction to any type of cue. However, a [[meta-analysis]] published in 2022 found that the [[effect size]]s of published studies testing for ocean acidification effects on fish behavior have declined by an order of magnitude over the past decade, and have been negligible for the past five years.<ref name="Clements e3001511">{{cite journal |last1=Clements |first1=Jeff C. |last2=Sundin |first2=Josefin |last3=Clark |first3=Timothy D. |last4=Jutfelt |first4=Fredrik |date=2022-02-03 |title=Meta-analysis reveals an extreme 'decline effect' in the impacts of ocean acidification on fish behavior |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=20 |issue=2 |article-number=e3001511 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.3001511 |pmc=8812914 |pmid=35113875 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Eel embryos, a "critically endangered" species<ref>Pike C, Crook V, GollockM. Anguilla anguilla. The IUCN Red List ofThreatened Species 2020: e. T60344A152845178. International Union for Conservation ofNature; 2020. https://doi.org/10.2305/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230223113152/https://doi.org/10.2305/ |date=23 February 2023}} IUCN.UK.2020-2.RLTS.T60344A152845178.en</ref> yet profound{{clarify|date=October 2023}} in aquaculture, are also being affected by ocean acidification, specifically the [[European eel]]. Although they spend most of their lives in fresh water, usually in rivers, streams, or estuaries, they go to spawn and die in the [[Sargasso Sea]]. Here is where European eels are experiencing the effects of acidification in one of their key life stages.

Fish embryos and larvae are usually more sensitive to pH changes than adults, as organs for pH regulation are not full developed.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brauner |first1=Colin J. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1546509819300093 |title=Acid-base physiology and {{CO2}} homeostasis: Regulation and compensation in response to elevated environmental {{CO2}} |last2=Shartau |first2=Ryan B. |last3=Damsgaard |first3=Christian |last4=Esbaugh |first4=Andrew J. |last5=Wilson |first5=Rod W. |last6=Grosell |first6=Martin |date=January 2019 |publisher=Academic Press |editor-last=Grosell |editor-first=Martin |volume=37 |pages=69–132 |doi=10.1016/bs.fp.2019.08.003 |eissn=1546-5098 |editor-last2=Munday |editor-first2=Philip L. |editor-last3=Farrell |editor-first3=Anthony P. |editor-last4=Brauner |editor-first4=Colin J.}}</ref> Because of this, European eel embryos are more vulnerable to changes in pH in the Sargasso Sea. A study of the European Eel in the Sargasso Sea was conducted in 2021 to analyze the specific effects of ocean acidification on embryos. The study found that exposure to predicted end-of-century ocean p{{CO2}} conditions may affect normal development of this species in nature during sensitive early life history stages with limited physiological response capacities, while extreme acidification would negatively influence embryonic survival and development under hatchery conditions.<ref>Sganga, Daniela E., et al. "{{CO2}}-Induced Seawater Acidification Impacts Survival and Development of European Eel Embryos." PLOS ONE, edited by Hans G. Dam, vol. 17, no. 4, Apr. 2022, p. e0267228. DOI.org (Crossref), https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0267228.</ref>

===Compounded effects of acidification, warming, and deoxygenation===
{{Further|Effects of climate change on oceans|Ocean deoxygenation}}
[[File:Drivers of hypoxia and acidification in upwelling shelf systems.svg|thumb|upright=1.7| Drivers of [[hypoxia (environmental)|hypoxia]] and ocean acidification intensification in [[upwelling]] shelf systems. Equatorward winds drive the upwelling of low [[dissolved oxygen]] (DO), high nutrient, and high [[dissolved inorganic carbon]] (DIC) water from above the [[oxygen minimum zone]]. Cross-shelf gradients in productivity and bottom water residence times drive the strength of DO (DIC) decrease (increase) as water transits across a productive [[continental shelf]].<ref name="Chan2019">{{cite journal |last1=Chan |first1=Francis |last2=Barth |first2=John |last3=Kroeker |first3=Kristy |last4=Lubchenco |first4=Jane |last5=Menge |first5=Bruce |date=1 September 2019 |title=The Dynamics and Impact of Ocean Acidification and Hypoxia: Insights from Sustained Investigations in the Northern California Current Large Marine Ecosystem |journal=Oceanography |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=62–71 |doi=10.5670/oceanog.2019.312 |s2cid=202922296 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Ocgpy..32c..62C}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] Material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=16 October 2017}}.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Gewin |first=Virginia |date=August 2010 |title=Oceanography: Dead in the water |journal=Nature |volume=466 |issue=7308 |pages=812–814 |doi=10.1038/466812a |pmid=20703282 |s2cid=4358903 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2010Natur.466..812G}}</ref>]]

There is a substantial body of research showing that a combination of ocean acidification and elevated [[ocean temperature]] have a compounded effect on marine life and the ocean environment. This effect far exceeds the individual harmful impact of either.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Beusen |first1=Arthur |last2=Breitburg |first2=Denise |last3=Comeau |first3=Steve |last4=Dupont |first4=Sam |last5=Isensee |first5=Kirsten |last6=Kudela |first6=Raphael M. |last7=Lundholm |first7=Nina |last8=Otto |first8=Saskia |last9=Schwing |first9=Franklin |last10=Tilbrook |first10=Bronte |last11=Hansen |first11=Per Juel |last12=Boyd |first12=Philip W. |date=2022 |others=UNESCO/IOC, UNESCO/IOC, Philip W. Boyd, Kirsten Isensee |title=Multiple Ocean Stressors: A scientific Summary for Policy Makers. |journal=IOC Information Series |publisher=Unesco-Ioc |doi=10.25607/OBP-1724 |number=1404 |page=16 |bibcode=2022ioc..data...16B |hdl=11329/1892}}</ref> In addition, ocean warming, along with increased productivity of phytoplankton from higher {{CO2}} levels exacerbates [[ocean deoxygenation]]. Deoxygenation of ocean waters is an additional stressor on marine organisms that increases [[ocean stratification]] therefore limiting nutrients over time and reducing biological gradients.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bednaršek |first1=N. |last2=Harvey |first2=C.J. |last3=Kaplan |first3=I.C. |last4=Feely |first4=R.A. |last5=Možina |first5=J. |year=2016 |title=Pteropods on the edge: Cumulative effects of ocean acidification, warming, and deoxygenation |journal=Progress in Oceanography |volume=145 |pages=1–24 |bibcode=2016PrOce.145....1B |doi=10.1016/j.pocean.2016.04.002}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keeling |first1=Ralph F. |last2=Garcia |first2=Hernan E. |year=2002 |title=The change in oceanic O<sub>2</sub> inventory associated with recent global warming |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=99 |issue=12 |pages=7848–7853 |bibcode=2002PNAS...99.7848K |doi=10.1073/pnas.122154899 |pmc=122983 |pmid=12048249 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Meta analyses have quantified the direction and magnitude of the harmful effects of combined ocean acidification, warming, and deoxygenation on the ocean.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gruber |first=Nicolas |date=2011-05-28 |title=Warming up, turning sour, losing breath: ocean biogeochemistry under global change |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |volume=369 |issue=1943 |pages=1980–1996 |bibcode=2011RSPTA.369.1980G |doi=10.1098/rsta.2011.0003 |pmid=21502171 |s2cid=836308}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anthony |first1=Kenneth R. N. |last2=Maynard |first2=Jeffrey A. |last3=Diaz-Pulido |first3=Guillermo |last4=Mumby |first4=Peter J. |last5=Marshall |first5=Paul A. |last6=Cao |first6=Long |last7=Hoegh-Guldberg |first7=Ove |date=2011 |title=Ocean acidification and warming will lower coral reef resilience |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=17 |issue=5 |pages=1798–1808 |bibcode=2011GCBio..17.1798A |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2486.2010.02364.x |pmc=3597261}}</ref> These meta-analyses have been further tested by [[mesocosm]] studies that simulated the interaction of these stressors and found a catastrophic effect on the marine food web: thermal stress more than negates any primary producer to herbivore increase in productivity from elevated {{CO2}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goldenberg |first1=Silvan U. |last2=Nagelkerken |first2=Ivan |last3=Ferreira |first3=Camilo M. |last4=Ullah |first4=Hadayet |last5=Connell |first5=Sean D. |date=2017 |title=Boosted food web productivity through ocean acidification collapses under warming |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=23 |issue=10 |pages=4177–4184 |doi=10.1111/gcb.13699 |pmid=28447365 |bibcode=2017GCBio..23.4177G |s2cid=8015698}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pistevos |first1=Jennifer C. A. |last2=Nagelkerken |first2=Ivan |last3=Rossi |first3=Tullio |last4=Olmos |first4=Maxime |last5=Connell |first5=Sean D. |date=2015 |title=Ocean acidification and global warming impair shark hunting behaviour and growth |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=16293 |bibcode=2015NatSR...516293P |doi=10.1038/srep16293  |doi-access=free|pmc=4642292 |pmid=26559327}}</ref>

==Impacts on the economy and societies==
The increase of ocean acidity decelerates the rate of calcification in salt water, leading to smaller and slower growing [[coral reef]]s which supports approximately 25% of marine life.<ref>{{cite web |title=Coral reefs |url=http://wwf.panda.org/our_work/oceans/coasts/coral_reefs/ |access-date=2019-05-06 |website=WWF |archive-date=22 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822003508/http://wwf.panda.org/our_work/oceans/coasts/coral_reefs/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":05">{{cite journal |last1=Fabry |first1=Victoria J. |last2=Seibel |first2=Brad A. |last3=Feely |first3=Richard A. |last4=Orr |first4=James C. |date=April 2008 |title=Impacts of ocean acidification on marine fauna and ecosystem processes |journal=ICES Journal of Marine Science |volume=65 |issue=3 |pages=414–432 |doi=10.1093/icesjms/fsn048}}</ref> Impacts are far-reaching from fisheries and coastal environments down to the deepest depths of the ocean.<ref name=":14"/> The increase in ocean acidity is not only killing the coral, but also the wildly diverse population of marine inhabitants which coral reefs support.<ref name=":72">{{cite journal |last1=Hoegh-Guldberg |first1=O. |last2=Mumby |first2=P. J. |last3=Hooten |first3=A. J. |last4=Steneck |first4=R. S. |last5=Greenfield |first5=P. |last6=Gomez |first6=E. |last7=Harvell |first7=C. D. |last8=Sale |first8=P. F. |last9=Edwards |first9=A. J. |last10=Caldeira |first10=K. |last11=Knowlton |first11=N. |last12=Eakin |first12=C. M. |last13=Iglesias-Prieto |first13=R. |last14=Muthiga |first14=N. |last15=Bradbury |first15=R. H. |date=14 December 2007 |title=Coral Reefs Under Rapid Climate Change and Ocean Acidification |journal=Science |volume=318 |issue=5857 |pages=1737–1742 |bibcode=2007Sci...318.1737H |doi=10.1126/science.1152509 |pmid=18079392 |s2cid=12607336 |hdl-access=free |last17=Hatziolos |last16=Dubi |first16=A. |first17=M. E. |hdl=1885/28834}}</ref>

===Fishing and tourism industry===
The threat of acidification includes a decline in [[commercial fishing|commercial fisheries]] and the coast-based [[tourism industry]]. Several ocean goods and services are likely to be undermined by future ocean acidification potentially affecting the livelihoods of some 470 to 870&nbsp;million of the world's poorest people, depending upon the [[Shared Socioeconomic Pathways|greenhouse gas emission scenario]].<ref name=":3"/>

Some 1&nbsp;billion people are completely or partially dependent on the fishing, tourism, and coastal management services provided by coral reefs. Ongoing acidification of the oceans may therefore threaten future [[food chains]] linked with the oceans.<ref name="auto"/><ref name=":18"/>

====Arctic====
In the Arctic, commercial fisheries are threatened because acidification harms calcifying organisms which form the base of the Arctic food webs (pteropods and brittle stars, see above). Acidification threatens Arctic food webs from the base up. Arctic food webs are considered simple, meaning there are few steps in the food chain from small organisms to larger predators. For example, pteropods are "a key prey item of a number of higher predators – larger plankton, fish, seabirds, whales".<ref>{{cite web |title=Antarctic marine wildlife is under threat, study finds |publisher=BBC Nature |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/nature/20461646 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121126140652/http://www.bbc.co.uk/nature/20461646 |archive-date=26 November 2012 |access-date=13 October 2013}}</ref> Both pteropods and sea stars serve as a substantial food source and their removal from the simple food web would pose a serious threat to the whole ecosystem. The effects on the calcifying organisms at the base of the food webs could potentially destroy fisheries.

====United Kingdom commercial fisheries====
The shellfish industry is an important part of the United Kingdom economy.<ref name=":21">{{cite journal |last=Mangi |first=Stephen |date=2018-05-25 |title=The economic impacts of ocean acidification on shellfish fisheries and aquaculture in the United Kingdom |website=doi.org |doi=10.31230/osf.io/d4wh7}}</ref> In 2013, the shellfish industry contributed 37% of total landings by value.<ref name=":21"/> England and Scotland are the highest producers of shellfish within the United Kingdom.<ref name=":21"/> It has been found that annually fishers catch 66,000 tons and 61,000 tons.<ref name=":21"/> In terms of value, the wild-captured shellfish are worth 203 million pounds per year.<ref name=":21"/> However, ocean acidification is causing a decrease in the growth of many shellfish species.<ref name=":21"/> This is causing a drastic economic loss in the United Kingdom economy.<ref name=":21"/>

It is predicted that by 2100 there will be an economy-wide economic loss of shellfish production in the United Kingdom.<ref name=":21"/> The direct potential loss ranges from 14 to 28 percent of fishery output.<ref name=":21"/> That is a total loss of about 23 to 88 million pounds.<ref name=":21"/> The financial losses vary regionally due to different patterns of wild-caught shellfish and the exploitation of species with differing sensitivities to ocean acidification.<ref name=":21"/> Shellfish resources in the United Kingdom will require regional, national, or international solutions to reduce the impacts of ocean acidification on shellfish species and stabilize the economy.<ref name=":21"/>

====US commercial fisheries====
[[File:R0023623 - Flickr - NOAA Photo Library.jpg|thumb|An adult [[American lobster]] rests on the sea floor. Rhode Island, Dutch Island, Newport County.]]
The value of fish caught from US commercial fisheries in 2007 was valued at $3.8&nbsp;billion and of that 73% was derived from calcifiers and their direct predators.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=V. J. Fabry |last2=C. Langdon |last3=W. M. Balch |last4=A. G. Dickson |last5=R. A. Feely |last6=B. Hales |last7=D. A. Hutchins |last8=J. A. Kleypas |last9=C. L. Sabine |name-list-style=amp |title=Present and Future Impacts of Ocean Acidification on Marine Ecosystems and Biogeochemical Cycles |url=http://www.us-ocb.org/publications/OCB_OA_rept.pdf |journal=Report of the Ocean Carbon and Biogeochemistry Scoping Workshop on Ocean Acidification Research |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101117232337/http://www.us-ocb.org/publications/OCB_OA_rept.pdf |archive-date=17 November 2010 |access-date=14 November 2013}}</ref> Other organisms are directly harmed as a result of acidification. For example, decrease in the growth of marine calcifiers such as the [[American lobster]], [[Arctica islandica|ocean quahog]], and [[scallop]]s means there is less shellfish meat available for sale and consumption.<ref>{{cite web |year=2012 |title=Canada's State of the Oceans Report, 2012 |url=http://dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/coe-cde/soto/report-rapport-2012/index-eng.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131106083015/http://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/science/coe-cde/soto/report-rapport-2012/index-eng.asp |archive-date=6 November 2013 |access-date=21 October 2013 |website=Report |publisher=Fisheries and Oceans Canada}}</ref> Red king crab fisheries are also at a serious threat because crabs are also calcifiers. Baby red king crab when exposed to increased acidification levels experienced 100% mortality after 95&nbsp;days.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Foy |first1=Robert J. |last2=Carls |first2=Mark |last3=Dalton |first3=Michael |last4=Hurst |first4=Tom |last5=Long |first5=W. Christopher |last6=Poljak |first6=Dusanka |last7=Punt |first7=André E. |last8=Sigler |first8=Michael F. |last9=Stone |first9=Robert P. |date=Winter 2013 |title=CO 2, pH, and Anticipating a Future under Ocean Acidification |url=http://www.afs-alaska.org/wp-content/uploads/Onco331.pdf |access-date=14 November 2013 |magazine=Oncorhynchus |volume=XXXIII |issue=1 |author10=Swiney, Katherine M. |archive-date=18 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418215109/http://www.afs-alaska.org/wp-content/uploads/Onco331.pdf}}</ref> In 2006, red king crab accounted for 23% of the total guideline harvest levels and a serious decline in red crab population would threaten the crab harvesting industry.<ref>{{cite web |date=November 2005 |title=Bering Sea Crab Fishery |url=http://www.alaskaseafood.org/fishingprocessing/seafoodweb/stories/crab.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211122841/http://www.alaskaseafood.org/fishingprocessing/seafoodweb/stories/crab.html |archive-date=11 December 2013 |access-date=10 November 2013 |website=Report |publisher=Seafood Market Bulletin}}</ref>

==Possible responses==
===Climate change mitigation===
{{Main|Climate change mitigation|Carbon dioxide removal|Carbon sequestration#Sequestration techniques in oceans}}

Reducing carbon dioxide emissions (i.e. [[climate change mitigation]] measures) is the only solution that addresses the root cause of ocean acidification. For example, some mitigation measures focus on [[carbon dioxide removal]] (CDR) from the atmosphere (e.g. [[direct air capture]] (DAC), [[bioenergy with carbon capture and storage]] (BECCS)). These would also slow the rate of acidification.

Approaches that remove carbon dioxide from the ocean include [[ocean fertilization|ocean nutrient fertilization]], [[artificial upwelling]] and/or downwelling, [[seaweed farming]], ecosystem recovery, ocean alkalinity enhancement, [[enhanced weathering]], and electrochemical processes.<ref name="AR6 WGIII Ch 12">IPCC (2022) [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Chapter_12.pdf Chapter 12: Cross sectoral perspectives] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221013122242/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_Chapter_12.pdf|date=13 October 2022}} in [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/ Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802125242/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/|date=2 August 2022}}, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US</ref>{{rp|12–36}} All of these methods use the ocean to remove {{CO2}} from the atmosphere to store it in the ocean. These methods could assist with mitigation but they can have side-effects on marine life. The research field for all CDR methods has grown a lot since 2019.<ref name=":10"/>

In total, "ocean-based methods have a combined potential to remove 1–100 gigatons of {{CO2}} per year".<ref name=":12">IPCC (2022) [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_TS.pdf Technical Summary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923091131/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_TS.pdf|date=23 September 2022}}. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/ Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802125242/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/|date=2 August 2022}}, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US</ref>{{rp|TS-94}} Their costs are in the order of {{val|p={{USD}}|40|–|500}} per ton of {{CO2}}. For example, [[enhanced weathering]] could remove {{val|2|–|4|ul=gigatons}} of {{CO2}} per year. This technology comes with a cost of {{val|50|–|200|p={{USD}}}} per ton of {{CO2}}.<ref name=":12"/>{{rp|TS-94}}

===Carbon removal technologies which add alkalinity===
{{See also|Carbon sequestration#Adding bases to neutralize acids}}
Some [[carbon removal]] techniques add alkalinity to the ocean and therefore immediately buffer pH changes which might help the organisms in the region that the extra alkalinity is added to. The two technologies that fall into this category are ocean alkalinity enhancement and electrochemical methods.<ref name=":10"/> Eventually, due to diffusion, that alkalinity addition will be quite small to distant waters. This is why the term ''local ocean acidification mitigation'' is used. Both of these technologies have the potential to operate on a large scale and to be efficient at removing carbon dioxide.<ref name=":10"/>{{rp|Table 9.1}} However, they are expensive, have many risks and side effects, and currently have a low [[technology readiness level]].<ref name="AR6 WGIII Ch 12"/>{{rp|12–36}}

====Ocean alkalinity enhancement====
Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) is a proposed "carbon dioxide removal (CDR) method that involves deposition of alkaline minerals or their dissociation products at the ocean surface".<ref name="IPCC AR6 WGI Glossary">IPCC, 2021: [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_AnnexVII.pdf Annex VII: Glossary] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220605175306/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGI_AnnexVII.pdf|date=5 June 2022}} [Matthews, J.B.R., V. Möller, R. van Diemen, J.S. Fuglestvedt, V. Masson-Delmotte, C. Méndez, S. Semenov, A. Reisinger (eds.)]. In [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/ Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210809131444/https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/|date=9 August 2021}} [Masson-Delmotte, V., P. Zhai, A. Pirani, S.L. Connors, C. Péan, S. Berger, N. Caud, Y. Chen, L. Goldfarb, M.I. Gomis, M. Huang, K. Leitzell, E. Lonnoy, J.B.R. Matthews, T.K. Maycock, T. Waterfield, O. Yelekçi, R. Yu, and B. Zhou (eds.)]. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, US</ref>{{rp|2241}} The process would increase surface total alkalinity. It would work to increase ocean absorption of {{CO2}}. The process involves increasing the amount of [[bicarbonate]] ({{chem2|HCO3-}}) through accelerated weathering ([[enhanced weathering]]) of rocks ([[silicate]], [[limestone]], and [[quicklime]]).<ref name=":10">{{cite book |title=A Research Strategy for Ocean-based Carbon Dioxide Removal and Sequestration |year=2022 |isbn=978-0-309-08761-2 |doi=10.17226/26278 |pmid=35533244 |s2cid=245089649}}</ref>{{rp|181}} This process mimics the silicate-carbonate cycle. The {{CO2}} either becomes bicarbonate, remaining in that form for more than 100 years, or may precipitate into calcium carbonate ({{chem2|CaCO3}}). When calcium carbonate is buried in the deep ocean, it can hold the carbon indefinitely when utilizing silicate rocks.

Enhanced weathering is one type of ocean alkalinity enhancement. Enhanced weathering increases alkalinity by scattering fine rock particles. This can happen on land and in the ocean (even though the outcome eventually affects the ocean).

In addition to sequestering {{CO2}}, alkalinity addition buffers the pH of the ocean therefore reducing ocean acidification. However, little is known about how organisms respond to added alkalinity, even from natural sources.<ref name=":10"/> For example, weathering of some silicate rocks could release a large amount of trace metals at the weathering site.

Cost and energy consumed by ocean alkalinity enhancement (mining, pulverizing, transport) is high compared to other CDR techniques.<ref name=":10"/> The cost is estimated to be {{val|20|–|50|p={{USD}}}} per ton of {{CO2}} (for "direct addition of alkaline minerals to the ocean").<ref name="AR6 WGIII Ch 12"/>{{rp|12–50}}

Carbon sequestered as bicarbonate in the ocean amounts to about 30% of carbon emissions since the [[Industrial Revolution]].

Experimental materials include limestone, [[brucite]], [[olivine]], and alkaline solutions. Another approach is to use electricity to raise alkalinity during desalination to capture waterborne {{CO2}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Cornwall |first=Warren |date=30 November 2023 |title=An Alkaline Solution |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/climate-crisis-sparks-effort-coax-oceans-suck-carbon-dioxide?et_cid=5008204&et_rid=49310172 |journal=Science Magazine |volume=382 |issue=6674 |pages=988–992 |doi=10.1126/science.adn1880 |pmid=38033057 |bibcode=2023Sci...382..988C |archive-date=4 December 2023 |access-date=4 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231204020009/https://www.science.org/content/article/climate-crisis-sparks-effort-coax-oceans-suck-carbon-dioxide?et_cid=5008204&et_rid=49310172 |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Electrochemical methods====
Electrochemical methods, or [[electrolysis]], can strip carbon dioxide directly from seawater.<ref name=":10"/> Electrochemical process are a type of ocean alkalinity enhancement, too. Some methods focus on direct {{CO2}} removal (in the form of carbonate and {{CO2}} gas) while others increase the alkalinity of seawater by precipitating metal hydroxide residues, which absorbs {{CO2}} in a matter described in the ocean alkalinity enhancement section. The hydrogen produced during direct carbon capture can then be upcycled to form hydrogen for energy consumption, or other manufactured laboratory reagents such as [[hydrochloric acid]].

However, implementation of electrolysis for carbon capture is expensive and the energy consumed for the process is high compared to other CDR techniques.<ref name=":10"/> In addition, research to assess the environmental impact of this process is ongoing. Some complications include toxic chemicals in wastewaters, and reduced DIC in effluents; both of these may negatively impact marine life.<ref name=":10"/>

==Policies and goals==
[[File:Save our ocean, People's Climate March, 29 April 2017 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Demonstrator calling for action against ocean acidification at the [[People's Climate March (2017)]]]]

===Global policies===
As awareness about ocean acidification grows, policies geared toward increasing monitoring efforts of ocean acidification have been drafted.<ref>{{cite web |title=Action Plans |url=https://www.oaalliance.org/action-plans |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=OA Alliance |language=en-US |archive-date=7 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230307073624/https://www.oaalliance.org/action-plans |url-status=live}}</ref> Previously in 2015, ocean scientist [[Jean-Pierre Gattuso]] had remarked that "The ocean has been minimally considered at previous climate negotiations. Our study provides compelling arguments for a radical change at the UN conference (in Paris) on climate change".<ref name=":1">{{cite news |last=Harrabin |first=Roger |date=3 July 2015 |title={{CO2}} emissions threaten ocean crisis |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-33369024 |publisher=BBC News |archive-date=26 January 2024 |access-date=21 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240126024920/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-33369024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

International efforts, such as the Wider Caribbean's [[Convention for the Protection and Development of the Marine Environment of the Wider Caribbean Region|Cartagena Convention]] (entered into force in 1986),<ref>{{cite web |title=Cartagena Convention {{!}} The Caribbean Environment Programme (CEP) |url=https://www.unep.org/cep/who-we-are/cartagena-convention |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=unep.org |archive-date=3 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103153812/https://www.unep.org/cep/who-we-are/cartagena-convention |url-status=live}}</ref> may enhance the support provided by regional governments to highly vulnerable areas in response to ocean acidification.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.unep.org/cep/news/editorial/cartagena-convention-secretariat-and-ocean-foundation-cooperate-priority-marine |title=Cartagena Convention Secretariat and The Ocean Foundation to cooperate on priority marine biodiversity and pollution issues |website=Caribbean Environment Programme |publisher=United Nations Environment Programme |access-date=4 September 2024 |date=12 November 2019}}</ref> Many countries, for example in the Pacific Islands and Territories, have constructed regional policies, or National Ocean Policies, National Action Plans, National Adaptation Plans of Action and Joint National Action Plans on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction, to help work toward [[Sustainable Development Goal 14|SDG 14]]. Ocean acidification is now starting to be considered within those frameworks.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Turner |first1=J |url=https://www.sprep.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/MainstreamingOAintoNationalPolicies_PacifcIslandsHandbook_0.pdf |title=Mainstreaming Ocean Acidification into National Policies: A Handbook for Pacific Islands |last2=McIntosh |first2=R. Duncan |publisher=Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme. |year=2019 |location=Apia, Samoa |archive-date=14 January 2024 |access-date=4 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240114215731/https://www.sprep.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/MainstreamingOAintoNationalPolicies_PacifcIslandsHandbook_0.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

====UN Ocean Decade====
{{See also|UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development}}
The UN Ocean Decade has a program called "Ocean acidification research for sustainability". It was proposed by the Global Ocean Acidification Observing Network (GOA-ON) and its partners, and has been formally endorsed as a program of the [[UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Ocean Decade – The Science we need for the Ocean we want |url=https://www.oceandecade.org/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=Ocean Decade |language=en-US |archive-date=15 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240215021752/https://oceandecade.org/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Overview |url=http://goa-on.org/oars/overview.php |website=OARS: Ocean Acidification Research for Sustainability |publisher=GOA-ON |access-date=4 November 2022 |archive-date=21 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231221153745/http://www.goa-on.org/oars/overview.php |url-status=live}}</ref> The OARS program builds on the work of GOA-ON and has the following aims: to further develop the science of ocean acidification; to increase observations of ocean chemistry changes; to identify the impacts on marine ecosystems on local and global scales; and to provide decision makers with the information needed to mitigate and adapt to ocean acidification.

====Global Climate Indicators====
The importance of ocean acidification is reflected in its inclusion as one of seven Global Climate Indicators.<ref>{{cite web |title=Global Climate Indicators |url=https://gcos.wmo.int/en/global-climate-indicators |website=GCOS |date=19 June 2024 |publisher=WMO |access-date=4 November 2022 |archive-date=28 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240128235515/https://gcos.wmo.int/en/global-climate-indicators |url-status=live}}</ref> These Indicators are a set of parameters that describe the changing climate without reducing climate change to only [[instrumental temperature record|rising temperature]]. The indicators include key information for the most relevant domains of climate change: temperature and energy, atmospheric composition, ocean and water as well as the cryosphere. The Global Climate Indicators have been identified by scientists and communication specialists in a process led by [[Global Climate Observing System]] (GCOS).<ref>{{cite web |title=Home {{!}} GCOS |url=https://gcos.wmo.int/en/home |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=gcos.wmo.int |archive-date=13 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240113010920/https://gcos.wmo.int/en/home |url-status=live}}</ref> The Indicators have been endorsed by the [[World Meteorological Organization]] (WMO). They form the basis of the annual WMO Statement of the State of the Global Climate, which is submitted to the [[Conferences of the Parties of UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol|Conference of Parties]] (COP) of the [[United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change]] (UNFCCC). Additionally, the [[Copernicus Climate Change Service]] (C3S) of the European Commission uses the Indicators for their annual "European State of the Climate".

====Sustainable Development Goal 14====
In 2015, the United Nations adopted the 2030 Agenda and a set of 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), including a goal dedicated to the ocean, [[Sustainable Development Goal 14]],<ref name=":5">{{cite web |title=Goal 14 targets |url=https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/oceans/ |access-date=2020-09-24 |website=UNDP |archive-date=9 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190409100208/https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/oceans/ |url-status=live}}</ref> which calls to "conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas, and marine resources for sustainable development". Ocean acidification is directly addressed by the target SDG 14.3. The full title of Target 14.3 is: "Minimize and address the impacts of ocean acidification, including through enhanced scientific cooperation at all levels".<ref name=":17">United Nations (2017) Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 6 July 2017, [[:File:A RES 71 313 E.pdf|Work of the Statistical Commission pertaining to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development]] ([https://undocs.org/A/RES/71/313 A/RES/71/313] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023121826/https://undocs.org/A/RES/71/313 |date=23 October 2020}})</ref> This target has one indicator: Indicator 14.3.1 which calls for the "Average marine acidity ([[pH]]) measured at agreed suite of representative sampling stations".<ref name=":42">{{cite web |title=Goal 14: Sustainable Development Knowledge Platform |url=https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/sdg14 |access-date=2020-09-05 |publisher=United Nations |archive-date=12 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190412130633/https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/sdg14 |url-status=live}}</ref>

The [[Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission]] (IOC) of [[UNESCO]] was identified as the custodian agency for the SDG 14.3.1 Indicator. In this role, IOC-UNESCO is tasked with developing the SDG 14.3.1 Indicator Methodology, the annual collection of data toward the SDG 14.3.1 Indicator and the reporting of progress to the United Nations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Update on IOC Custodianship Role in Relation to SDG 14 Indicators |url=https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000265127.locale=en |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=unesdoc.unesco.org |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031132927/https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000265127.locale=en |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=SDG 14.3.1 data portal |url=https://oa.iode.org/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=oa.iode.org |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031133402/https://oa.iode.org/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Policies at country level===
====United States====
In the United States, the Federal Ocean Acidification Research And Monitoring Act of 2009 supports government coordination, such as the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration|National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration]]'s (NOAA) "Ocean Acidification Program".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Galdies |first1=Charles |last2=Bellerby |first2=Richard |last3=Canu |first3=Donata |last4=Chen |first4=Wenting |last5=Garcia-Luque |first5=Enrique |last6=Gašparović |first6=Blaženka |last7=Godrijan |first7=Jelena |last8=Lawlor |first8=Paul J. |last9=Maes |first9=Frank |last10=Malej |first10=Alenka |last11=Panagiotaras |first11=Dionisios |last12=Romera |first12=Beatriz Martinez |last13=Reymond |first13=Claire E. |last14=Rochette |first14=Julien |last15=Solidoro |first15=Cosimo |date=2020-08-01 |title=European policies and legislation targeting ocean acidification in european waters – Current state |journal=Marine Policy |volume=118 |article-number=103947 |doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2020.103947 |s2cid=218961473 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020MarPo.11803947G}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=OAP Home |url=https://oceanacidification.noaa.gov/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=oceanacidification.noaa.gov |archive-date=15 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240215055846/https://oceanacidification.noaa.gov/ |url-status=live}}</ref> In 2015, USEPA denied a citizens petition that asked EPA to regulate {{CO2}} under the [[Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976]] in order to mitigate ocean acidification.<ref>{{cite web |author=Center for Biological Diversity |author2=Donn J. Viviani |title=TSCA Section 21 Petition Requesting EPA to Regulate Anthropogenic Emissions Carbon Dioxide |url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-09/documents/petition_oa_tsca_2014_final_2.pdf |website=US EPA |access-date=6 July 2025 |archive-date=6 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250706014013/https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-09/documents/petition_oa_tsca_2014_final_2.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2015-10-07 |title=Carbon Dioxide Emissions and Ocean Acidification; TSCA Section 21 Petition; Reasons for Agency Response |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2015/10/07/2015-25164/carbon-dioxide-emissions-and-ocean-acidification-tsca-section-21-petition-reasons-for-agency#page-60577 |publisher=Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) |pages=60577–60584 |access-date=24 June 2017 |archive-date=24 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210924162909/https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2015/10/07/2015-25164/carbon-dioxide-emissions-and-ocean-acidification-tsca-section-21-petition-reasons-for-agency#page-60577 |url-status=live}}</ref> In the denial, the EPA said that risks from ocean acidification were being "more efficiently and effectively addressed" under domestic actions, e.g., under the [[Presidential Climate Action Plan]], and that multiple avenues are being pursued to work with and in other nations to reduce emissions and deforestation and promote clean energy and energy efficiency.<ref>{{cite web |date=June 2013 |title=The President's Climate Action Plan |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/default/files/image/president27sclimateactionplan.pdf |publisher=obamawhitehouse.archives.gov |access-date=24 June 2017 |archive-date=1 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240201005452/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/default/files/image/president27sclimateactionplan.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==
Research into the phenomenon of ocean acidification, as well as awareness raising about the problem, has been going on for several decades. The fundamental research really began with the creation of the [[pH scale]] by [[Danish people|Danish]] chemist [[Søren Peder Lauritz Sørensen]] in 1909.<ref name="Sørensen">{{cite journal |last=Sørensen |first=S. P. L. |year=1909 |title=Über die Messung und die Bedeutung der Wasserstoffionenkonzentration bei enzymatischen Prozessen |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/14517358.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Biochem. Z. |volume=21 |pages=131–304 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210415205740/https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/14517358.pdf |archive-date=15 April 2021 |access-date=22 March 2021 |quote=Original German: Für die Zahl p schlage ich den Namen Wasserstoffionenexponent und die Schreibweise p<sub>H</sub>• vor. Unter dem Wasserstoffionexponenten (p<sub>H</sub>•) einer Lösungwird dann der Briggsche Logarithmus des reziproken Wertes des auf Wasserstoffionenbezagenen Normalitäts faktors de Lösungverstanden.}} Two other publications appeared in 1909, one in French and one in Danish.</ref> By around the 1950s the massive role of the ocean in absorbing fossil fuel {{CO2}} was known to specialists, but not appreciated by the greater scientific community.<ref name=":16"/> Throughout much of the 20th century, the dominant focus has been the beneficial process of oceanic {{CO2}} uptake, which has enormously ameliorated climate change. The concept of "too much of a good thing" has been late in developing and was triggered only by some key events, and the [[carbon sink|oceanic sink]] for heat and {{CO2}} is still critical as the primary buffer against climate change.<ref name=":16">{{cite journal |last=Brewer |first=P. G. |date=2013 |title=A short history of ocean acidification science in the 20th century: a chemist's view |url=https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/10/7411/2013/ |journal=Biogeosciences |language=English |volume=10 |issue=11 |pages=7411–7422 |bibcode=2013BGeo...10.7411B |doi=10.5194/bg-10-7411-2013 |issn=1726-4170 |doi-access=free |archive-date=4 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231104211459/https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/10/7411/2013/ |url-status=live}} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50x50px]] Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [[creativecommons:by/3.0/|Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported License]]</ref>

In the early 1970s questions over the long-term impact of the accumulation of fossil fuel {{CO2}} in the sea were already arising around the world and causing strong debate. Researchers commented on the accumulation of fossil {{CO2}} in the atmosphere and sea and drew attention to the possible impacts on marine life. By the mid-1990s, the likely impact of {{CO2}} levels rising so high with the inevitable changes in pH and carbonate ion became a concern of scientists studying the fate of coral reefs.<ref name=":16"/>

By the end of the 20th century the trade-offs between the beneficial role of the ocean in absorbing some 90% of all heat created, and the accumulation of some 50% of all fossil fuel {{CO2}} emitted, and the impacts on marine life were becoming more clear. By 2003, the time of planning for the "First Symposium on the Ocean in a High-{{CO2}} World" meeting to be held in Paris in 2004, many new research results on ocean acidification were published.<ref name=":16"/>

In 2009, members of the [[InterAcademy Panel]] called on world leaders to "Recognize that reducing the build up of {{CO2}} in the atmosphere is the only practicable solution to mitigating ocean acidification".<ref name="iap statement">{{cite web |author=IAP |date=June 2009 |title=Interacademy Panel (IAP) Member Academies Statement on Ocean Acidification |url=https://www.interacademies.org/statement/iap-statement-ocean-acidification |access-date=16 November 2020 |archive-date=29 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211029170810/https://www.interacademies.org/statement/iap-statement-ocean-acidification |url-status=live}}, Secretariat: TWAS (the Academy of Sciences for the Developing World), Trieste, Italy.</ref> The statement also stressed the importance to "Reinvigorate action to reduce stressors, such as [[overfishing]] and [[marine pollution|pollution]], on [[marine ecosystem]]s to increase resilience to ocean acidification".<ref>{{cite news |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2019-12-04 |title=Tackling degraded oceans could mitigate climate crisis – report |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/dec/04/tackling-ocean |access-date=2019-12-07 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |archive-date=27 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230327213313/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2019/dec/04/tackling-ocean |url-status=live}}</ref>

For example, research in 2010 found that in the 15-year period 1995–2010 alone, acidity had increased 6 percent in the upper 100&nbsp;meters of the Pacific Ocean from Hawaii to Alaska.<ref name="2010aug_sciam"/>

According to a statement in July 2012 by [[Jane Lubchenco]], head of the U.S. [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]] "surface waters are changing much more rapidly than initial calculations have suggested. It's yet another reason to be very seriously concerned about the amount of carbon dioxide that is in the atmosphere now and the additional amount we continue to put out."<ref name="HPost">{{cite web |date=9 July 2012 |title=Ocean Acidification Is Climate Change's 'Equally Evil Twin', NOAA Chief Says |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/07/09/ocean-acidification-reefs-climate-change_n_1658081.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120712003629/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/07/09/ocean-acidification-reefs-climate-change_n_1658081.html |archive-date=12 July 2012 |access-date=2012-07-09 |website=[[Huffington Post]]}}</ref>

A 2013 study found acidity was increasing at a rate 10 times faster than in any of the evolutionary crises in Earth's history.<ref>{{cite web |last=Harvey |first=Fiona |author-link=Fiona Harvey |date=2013-08-25 |title=Rising levels of acids in seas may endanger marine life, says study |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2013/aug/25/rising-acid-levels-seas-endanger-marine-poertner |access-date=2013-08-29 |website=The Guardian |archive-date=31 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231031134830/https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2013/aug/25/rising-acid-levels-seas-endanger-marine-poertner |url-status=live}}</ref>

The "Third Symposium on the Ocean in a High-{{CO2}} World" took place in Monterey, California, in 2012. The summary for policy makers from the conference stated that "Ocean acidification research is growing rapidly".<ref name="ocean"/>

In a synthesis report published in ''Science'' in 2015, 22 leading marine scientists stated that {{CO2}} from burning fossil fuels is changing the oceans' chemistry more rapidly than at any time since the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event|Great Dying]] (Earth's most severe known extinction event).<ref name=":1"/> Their report emphasized that the 2&nbsp;°C maximum temperature increase agreed upon by governments reflects too small a cut in emissions to prevent "dramatic impacts" on the world's oceans.<ref name=":1"/>

A study done in 2020 argues that ocean acidification is not only negatively affecting marine life, but also human health. Food quality, respiratory issues, and human health are all negatively affected by ocean acidification.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Falkenberg |first1=Laura J. |last2=Bellerby |first2=Richard G. J. |last3=Connell |first3=Sean D. |last4=Fleming |first4=Lora E. |last5=Maycock |first5=Bruce |last6=Russell |first6=Bayden D. |last7=Sullivan |first7=Francis J. |last8=Dupont |first8=Sam |date=2020-06-24 |title=Ocean Acidification and Human Health |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |language=en |volume=17 |issue=12 |page=4563 |doi=10.3390/ijerph17124563 |issn=1660-4601 |pmc=7344635 |pmid=32599924 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2020IJERP..17.4563F}}</ref>
